docs.title: Hax — Heterogeneity Analysis for CryoEM
docs.text:
A suite of GPU-accelerated tools to study conformational heterogeneity in Cryo-EM data. Estimate the continuous motions of your macromolecules, build and merge conformational landscapes, and reconstruct motion-corrected volumes — all from a single command line.

Get Started Browse Programs View Workflows

docs.title: What is Hax?
docs.text:
When a protein or molecular machine is imaged with Cryo-EM, every particle is a snapshot of the molecule frozen in a slightly different shape (or conformation). Classical reconstruction averages these snapshots into a single rigid map — and in doing so, it blurs away the very motions that make the molecule biologically interesting.

Hax is a collection of tools designed to recover that lost information. It uses modern neural networks (built on JAX + Flax) to learn how your molecule moves, to place every particle on a map of conformations (a conformational landscape), and to turn that landscape back into 3D structures you can inspect.

You do not need to be a machine-learning expert to use Hax. Every tool is a single command, the defaults are sensible, and this documentation explains each option in plain language.

New to conformational heterogeneity?

Start with the Core Concepts page. It introduces the handful of ideas — latent spaces, the CTF, metadata files, training modes — that show up across every Hax program.

docs.title: What can it do?
docs.text:
• Analyze motions

    Recover continuous conformational changes with HetSIREN, Zernike3Deep and ReconSIREN.

    Heterogeneity analysis

  • Merge landscapes

    Reconcile results from several methods into a single consensus space with FlexConsensus.

    FlexConsensus

  • Explore interactively

    Navigate your landscape and generate volumes in real time with the Annotate Space viewer.

    Annotate Space

  • Reconstruct without blur

    Build motion-corrected volumes that remove the smearing caused by flexibility, with MoDART.

    MoDART

docs.title: Install in one line
docs.text:
CUDA 12CUDA 13 
pip install hax-em[cuda12]

pip install hax-em[cuda13]

CUDA itself is installed for you — you only need a recent NVIDIA driver (≥ 525). See the full installation guide for the recommended Conda setup.

Two ways to run Hax

Use the command line, or run every program from your browser with the optional Hax GUI. After installing, you can verify everything works with the built-in test suite.

docs.title: A typical session
docs.text:
# 1. See what is available
hax_project_manager -h

# 2. Learn the conformational landscape of your particles
hax_project_manager --gpu 0 zernike3deep \
    --md particles.xmd --vol reference.mrc --sr 1.5 \
    --ctf_type apply --mode train --output_path results/

# 3. Explore the landscape interactively
hax_project_manager annotate_space \
    --z_space results/predicted_latents.xmd --path annotation/

Ready to dive in? Head to Getting Started, or jump straight to the Programs overview.

docs.title: How to cite Hax
docs.text: If Hax is useful in your research, please cite the relevant method(s). The full reference list — Zernike3D, HetSIREN, ZART/MoDART and FlexConsensus — is on the Contact & Support page.

docs.title: The Command Line
docs.text:
Everything in Hax is launched through a single command: hax_project_manager. It is a dispatcher — you tell it which program you want to run, on which GPU, and then pass that program's own arguments.

Prefer a graphical interface?

Everything on this page can also be done from your browser with the optional Hax GUI (hax-em-gui), which turns each program into an auto-generated form.

docs.title: The general pattern
docs.text:
hax_project_manager [--gpu <ids>] <program> [program arguments...]
  • --gpu <ids> — (optional) which GPU(s) Hax is allowed to use.
  • <program> — the name of the Hax tool to run (e.g. hetsiren, zernike3deep, modart).
  • program arguments — everything after the program name is handed straight to that program (e.g. --md, --sr, --mode…).

docs.title: Discovering what is available
docs.text:
List every program with a one-line description:

hax_project_manager -h

Get the full, detailed help for a single program — including every parameter and what it does:

hax_project_manager <program> -h

For example:

hax_project_manager hetsiren -h

This documentation mirrors the built-in help

Each program page in this site expands on the same help text you get from -h, with extra explanation and examples. The -h output is always the authoritative source for the exact version you have installed.

docs.title: Choosing a GPU with --gpu
docs.text:
If your machine has more than one GPU, use --gpu to pick which one(s) Hax runs on. The value is a comma-separated list of GPU indices (as shown by nvidia-smi).

# Run only on GPU 0
hax_project_manager --gpu 0 hetsiren ...

# Allow GPUs 0 and 1
hax_project_manager --gpu 0,1 hetsiren ...

Why the flag comes before the program name

--gpu sets the CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES environment variable before Hax imports JAX. That ordering is required for the GPU restriction to take effect, which is why --gpu must appear between hax_project_manager and the program name — not among the program's own arguments.

docs.title: Reusing parameters with --config
docs.text:
Every program accepts a --config option pointing at a YAML or JSON file whose keys are argument names without the leading --:

# my_run.yml
sr: 1.5
ctf_type: apply
epochs: 80
batch_size: 16

hax_project_manager --gpu 0 hetsiren --config my_run.yml --md particles.xmd --output_path run/

Values from the file act as defaults; anything you also pass on the command line overrides them. On every run the fully-resolved parameters are written to <output_path>/run_config.json, and that file can itself be reused as a --config to reproduce the run exactly.

docs.title: What the dispatcher sets up for you
docs.text:
When you launch a program, hax_project_manager automatically configures a few things so you don't have to:

  • Restricts the visible GPUs to those you passed with --gpu.
  • Disables JAX/XLA memory pre-allocation (XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_PREALLOCATE=false) so the process only grabs the GPU memory it actually needs.
  • Enables a set of XLA performance flags.
  • Silences low-level TensorFlow/XLA log spam.

docs.title: A first end-to-end command
docs.text:
A complete invocation looks like this:

hax_project_manager --gpu 0 zernike3deep \
    --md particles.xmd \
    --vol reference.mrc \
    --sr 1.5 \
    --ctf_type apply \
    --mode train \
    --output_path results/

Read this as: "On GPU 0, run zernike3deep in training mode on these particles and this reference volume, saving everything to results/."

If many of these options (--md, --sr, --ctf_type, --mode, --output_path…) look unfamiliar, the next page — Core Concepts — explains the ideas they all share before you reach the individual program pages.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text: Almost every Hax program shares the same handful of ideas and command-line options. Read this page once and the individual program pages will feel familiar.

docs.title: Conformational heterogeneity
docs.text:
Macromolecules are not rigid — they bend, twist, open and close as they work. In a Cryo-EM experiment, each particle image captures the molecule in one of these many shapes. The collection of all the shapes your molecule can adopt is its conformational heterogeneity.

  • Continuous heterogeneity — smooth, gradual motion (a hinge slowly closing).
  • Discrete heterogeneity — a few distinct states (bound vs. unbound).

Hax focuses primarily on recovering and describing continuous motion, while still letting you pick out discrete states from the result.

docs.title: The latent space (your "map of shapes")
docs.text:
Hax describes every particle by a short list of numbers called a latent vector. Think of it as the molecule's coordinates on a map of all its possible shapes. Particles with similar shapes sit close together on this map; very different shapes sit far apart. The map itself is the latent space (also called the conformational landscape).

  • --lat_dim sets how many numbers describe each shape (the dimensionality of the latent space). More dimensions can capture more complex motion but are harder to interpret and visualize. A typical starting value is small (e.g. 8 for the heterogeneity networks, 3 when you want something you can plot directly).

Once you have a latent space you can explore it (Annotate Space), clean it (Filter Latents), merge several of them (FlexConsensus), or turn points back into 3D volumes (Decode States from Latents).

docs.title: Metadata files (.xmd / .star / .cs)
docs.text:
Hax never reads raw images on their own — it reads a metadata file that lists your particle images together with the information needed to interpret them: their pose (orientation), shifts (centering), and CTF parameters.

Hax reads the three most common formats directly, so you can plug it into almost any pipeline without converting your files first:

  • .xmd — Xmipp metadata format.
  • .star — Relion/RELION-style metadata format.
  • .cs — CryoSPARC metadata format, read directly (support is provided through the xmipp_metadata library that Hax builds on).

You point Hax at one of these with the --md option. The images themselves are referenced from inside the metadata file, so they must remain accessible at the paths it records.

Where do these files come from?

Metadata files are produced by upstream Cryo-EM packages (CryoSPARC, Xmipp, Relion, Scipion, …) during particle picking, 2D/3D classification and refinement. Hax consumes the output of that pipeline.

Coming from CryoSPARC?

You can pass a CryoSPARC .cs file straight to --md — there is no need to export it to a .star file first.

docs.title: Sampling rate (--sr)
docs.text:
The sampling rate (also called pixel size) is the physical size of one pixel, in ångströms per pixel (Å/px). It is how Hax relates pixels to real-world distances.

  • Supplied with --sr (a number, e.g. 1.5).
  • It must match the images and reference volume you provide. Getting it wrong throws off every distance-dependent calculation (the CTF, the geometry of motion, resolution).

docs.title: The CTF and --ctf_type
docs.text:
The Contrast Transfer Function (CTF) describes how the microscope's optics distort the recorded image — it modulates and partially inverts the contrast at different spatial frequencies. To get faithful results, this distortion has to be accounted for.

The --ctf_type option tells Hax how to handle it:

Value What it does When to use it None Ignore the CTF entirely. Only for already CTF-corrected data, or quick tests. apply Apply the CTF to the generated projections so they match the (uncorrected) experimental images. The usual, robust choice for raw experimental particles. wiener CTF-correct the experimental images using a Wiener filter. When you prefer to correct the data side. precorrect Use a pre-correction of the experimental images. Alternative correction strategy.

If in doubt, apply is the most common and safe default for standard experimental particles.

docs.title: Masks (--mask)
docs.text:
A mask is a binary 3D volume (1 inside a region, 0 outside) that tells Hax where to focus. Masks let you concentrate the analysis on the part of the molecule you care about and ignore noisy or static regions.

  • For reconstruction masks, define the region to cover all the volume where the motions of interest happen.
  • Masks must usually be binary. Check each program page for whether a mask is required, optional, or generated automatically when omitted.

docs.title: Training modes: train and predict
docs.text:
The neural-network programs work in distinct modes, selected with --mode:

  • train — Learn from your data, building (training) a network from scratch, or continuing from a previous run if you also pass --reload. This is the step that actually fits the conformational landscape.
  • predict — Use an already-trained network to compute results (e.g. the latent vector of every particle) for a dataset. Requires --reload to point at the trained network.

A normal session is therefore: train once, then predict as many times as you need. The network saved by a train run can also be reused directly by post-processing tools such as Decode States from Latents and Estimate Latent Covariances.

docs.title: Saving and reloading (--output_path, --reload)
docs.text:
• --output_path — the folder where a program writes everything: the trained network, new metadata, predicted latents, volumes, training metrics, and so on. Each program page lists exactly what it produces.
  • --reload — the path to a previously saved network. Use it to:
    • continue / fine-tune a training run,
    • run predict (where it is mandatory).

Checkpoints make training resumable

During training, Hax periodically writes an intermediate checkpoint (e.g. *_CHECKPOINT/). If a run is interrupted, you can resume it by pointing --reload at the output of the previous run instead of starting over.

docs.title: Common training knobs
docs.text:
These options appear on most network programs and behave the same way everywhere:

Option Meaning Practical advice --epochs How many times the network sees the whole dataset. ~50–100 is enough for ≈100k particles; scale up/down with dataset size. --batch_size How many images are on the GPU at once. The main lever for GPU-memory usage — lower it if you run out of memory; watch with nvidia-smi. Very large batches can miss very local motions. --learning_rate The "step size" of learning. Default 1e-4 is a good start. If training produces NaNs or blows up, make it ~10× smaller. --dataset_split_fraction How data is split into training/validation subsets, as train,val. Defaults to 0.8,0.2. The two fractions must sum to 1. The validation subset is only used to measure accuracy, never to train.

docs.title: Reading data: RAM vs. memory-mapping
docs.text:
Cryo-EM datasets can be huge. Each program lets you choose how images are loaded:

  • --load_images_to_ram — load all images into RAM. Fastest, but only if the dataset fits in memory.
  • If you omit that flag, images are memory-mapped from disk instead. This trades a little speed (and some temporary disk space during the run) for a much smaller memory footprint. The temporary disk space is reclaimed when the run finishes.
  • --ssd_scratch_folder — when memory-mapping, point this at a folder on a fast SSD to read data faster. Highly recommended if you are not loading to RAM.

docs.title: Monitoring training
docs.text:
While a network trains, Hax writes metrics (loss curves, validation curves, sample volume slices) into a metrics folder inside your --output_path. You can watch these live — including after the run — with the Display Metrics program, which launches a TensorBoard dashboard in your browser.

With these concepts in hand, head to the Programs overview to find the right tool for your task.

docs.title: The Hax GUI
docs.text:
Prefer clicking to typing? The Hax GUI (hax-em-gui) is a modern web interface that lets you run every Hax program from your browser — with friendly auto-generated forms, a job manager with live logs, a server file browser, GPU selection and an embedded TensorBoard.

It runs on the GPU server and is reached from any browser, on any machine — no desktop install, no Node, no build step.

A separate, optional package

The GUI ships as its own package, hax-em-gui. It is optional: everything it does can also be done from the command line. Install it on top of an environment that already has hax-em.

New and actively developed

The GUI is a recent addition. Core features — the program launcher, job console, file browser and TensorBoard embedding — are in place. Interactive annotate_space 3D visualization and a visual workflow builder are on the roadmap.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
• Auto-generated forms for all Hax programs. Each program's command-line options become labelled fields (with the same help text you see on the program pages), so you never have to remember flag names.
  • A job manager — launch runs, watch live logs stream in, and revisit past jobs.
  • A server file browser for picking input metadata, volumes and masks without typing paths.
  • GPU selection discovered from nvidia-smi.
  • Embedded TensorBoard for display_metrics, so training curves appear right inside the GUI.
  • Projects & output folders — organize runs per project, each with its own output folder.

The frontend is intentionally build-tool-free (plain ES modules + hand-written CSS served directly by the backend), so there is no npm/node_modules supply chain and the browser only ever talks to your server.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A working hax-em installation in a Conda environment (see Installation). The GUI launches your programs through hax_project_manager, so it must run in (or be able to reach) that environment.
  • Python ≥ 3.10.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
In the same Conda environment that has hax-em installed:

From PyPIFrom a clone (development) 
pip install hax-em-gui

git clone https://github.com/DavidHerreros/hax-em-gui.git
cd hax-em-gui
pip install -e .

This installs the backend dependencies (FastAPI, Uvicorn…) and the hax-gui command. The web interface and a seed schema cache are bundled inside the package, so plain, editable and pip install git+<url> installs all work out of the box.

docs.title: Refresh the program schemas (recommended)
docs.text:
The GUI builds its forms from a cached description of each program's CLI. A seed cache ships with the package; regenerate it whenever a Hax program's options change:

hax-gui schemas        # from a clone: python backend/scripts/generate_schemas.py

Tip

Schema generation imports JAX (to introspect the programs), so it is not run automatically. Run it once after installing, and again after upgrading hax-em.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
The hax-gui command manages the server:

hax-gui start                 # start in the background on http://127.0.0.1:8000
hax-gui status                # is it running? where? (pid + health)
hax-gui restart               # relaunch, keeping the current host/port
hax-gui stop                  # stop it

Useful flags for hax-gui start:

Flag Purpose --host 0.0.0.0 Listen on all interfaces so other machines can connect. --port 8051 Use a different port. --foreground Run attached to the terminal (instead of in the background). --reload Auto-reload on code edits (development).

Then open http://<server>:<port> in any browser. Because the page and the API share an origin, there is no CORS or proxy to configure for local use.

Classic launch still works

If you prefer, you can start the backend directly with uvicorn hax_gui.app:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000.

docs.title: A typical GUI session
docs.text:
1. Open the GUI at http://<server>:<port> and pick (or create) a project.
  2. Choose a program from the catalog — the programs are grouped exactly like the Programs overview.
  3. Fill in the form. Use the file browser to select your --md metadata, reference volume and mask; pick a GPU; set options like --sr, --ctf_type and --mode.
  4. Launch the job and watch the live log in the job console.
  5. For training runs, open the TensorBoard tab to follow loss/validation curves (this is display_metrics embedded in the GUI).
  6. Find outputs in the project's per-run output folder, ready for the next step in your workflow.

docs.title: Configuration (backend environment variables)
docs.text:
For most local use the defaults are fine. For remote/server deployments you can tune:

Variable Default Purpose HAX_GUI_DATA_DIR ~/.hax_gui SQLite database + per-job log files. HAX_GUI_SCHEMA_CACHE (bundled cache) Path to the cached program form-schemas. HAX_PROJECT_MANAGER hax_project_manager The launcher command (supports multi-token, e.g. python -m hax.cli). HAX_GUI_FILE_ROOTS $HOME Colon-separated roots the file browser is allowed to expose. HAX_GUI_TOKEN (empty) Shared bearer token; empty means open — dev only. HAX_GUI_CORS_ORIGINS localhost:5173 Allowed dev SPA origins.

docs.title: Remote use & security
docs.text:
The backend is meant to run on the GPU server while the browser can be anywhere. The current model is single-tenant: protect it with a shared token (HAX_GUI_TOKEN) behind TLS, and put a reverse proxy (Caddy or nginx) in front to terminate TLS and route the API, the WebSocket and the web app.

Do not expose an untokenized GUI to a network

With an empty HAX_GUI_TOKEN the GUI is open to anyone who can reach the port, and it can launch jobs and browse files within the configured roots. Only run it that way on 127.0.0.1, and always set a token (and TLS) before exposing it beyond localhost.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Hax (hax-em on PyPI) is a pure-Python package. All of its heavy numerics run on the GPU through JAX and CUDA, so a CUDA-capable NVIDIA GPU is required to use it in practice.

Hardware & driver requirements

  • An NVIDIA GPU (the more VRAM, the larger the box sizes and batches you can handle).
  • NVIDIA driver ≥ 525. You do not need to install CUDA yourself — the correct CUDA 12 or CUDA 13 runtime is installed automatically together with the package.
  • A Linux environment is recommended.

docs.title: 1. Create a dedicated Conda environment (recommended)
docs.text:
Python is pinned to ≥ 3.11, < 3.12. Installing Hax inside its own Conda environment keeps its tightly-pinned dependencies (JAX, Flax, cuML, cupy…) from clashing with anything else on your system.

conda create -n hax python=3.11
conda activate hax

docs.title: 2. Install the package
docs.text:
Pick the command that matches the CUDA major version you want. If you are unsure, CUDA 12 is the safe choice on most current systems.

CUDA 12CUDA 13 
pip install hax-em[cuda12]

pip install hax-em[cuda13]

The [cuda12] / [cuda13] part is an extra — it pulls in JAX, cuML and cupy built for that CUDA version. Installing hax-em without an extra will not give you a working GPU setup.

docs.title: 3. Install from source (optional)
docs.text:
If you prefer a local, editable copy — for example to follow development or modify the code — clone the repository and install from inside it:

git clone https://github.com/DavidHerreros/hax-em.git
cd hax-em
pip install .[cuda12]   # or .[cuda13]

docs.title: 4. Verify the installation
docs.text:
After installation a single command becomes available: hax_project_manager. Confirm it works by listing the available programs:

hax_project_manager -h

You should see a summary of every Hax program. If you do, you are ready to go — continue to The Command Line to learn how launching works.

Want a thorough check?

To confirm the whole GPU stack (JAX, CUDA, cuML…) works end to end — not just that the CLI imports — run the built-in test suite on a synthetic phantom. See Verify Your Installation.

Prefer a graphical interface?

There is an optional web GUI, hax-em-gui, that lets you run every program from your browser. See The Hax GUI.

Working in Scipion?

The scipion-em-hax plugin installs Hax in its own environment and exposes the programs as Scipion protocols. See Using Hax from Scipion.

If JAX cannot see your GPU

If programs run very slowly or report that no GPU was found:

  • Check your driver with nvidia-smi (it must report driver version ≥ 525).
  • Make sure you installed the matching CUDA extra for your system.
  • Confirm you did not accidentally restrict the visible GPUs (see the --gpu flag on the CLI page).

docs.title: Using Hax from Scipion
docs.text:
Already process your data in Scipion? The Scipion plugin (scipion-em-hax) adds the Hax programs to Scipion's Flexibility Hub as ordinary protocols. You pick your particles, reference map and mask from the project, fill in a form, and the plugin converts the data, runs the Hax program and brings the results back as Scipion objects, ready for the next protocol.

A separate, optional package

The plugin ships as its own package, scipion-em-hax. It runs the same programs described on the program pages: each protocol builds the equivalent command line and launches it through hax_project_manager. Use whichever front end suits you: the plugin, the command line or the Hax GUI.

Why use the plugin?

  • No manual conversion. Particles from RELION, cryoSPARC or Xmipp refinements are passed in directly, with their CTF and poses. You never write --md or --sr yourself.
  • Chaining. Outputs (particles with latent vectors, volumes, classes) feed straight into other Scipion protocols, from Hax or from any other package.
  • Provenance. Every run, its parameters and its log are recorded in the project.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A working Scipion 3 installation.
  • Conda available to Scipion. The plugin creates its own environment for Hax.
  • An NVIDIA driver ≥ 525 on the machine that installs the plugin (see Installation). You do not need to install CUDA yourself.
  • The Xmipp plugin (scipion-em-xmipp). The Hax protocols use it to convert metadata and to resize images, volumes and masks.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Plugin manager / command lineFrom a clone (development)

Install from the Scipion Plugin manager, or from a terminal:

scipion3 installp -p scipion-em-hax

git clone https://github.com/scipion-em/scipion-em-hax.git
scipion3 installp -p ./scipion-em-hax --devel

In development mode hax-em itself is installed in editable mode from its devel branch, with the sources placed under Scipion's EM_ROOT folder.

The commands above assume scipion3 is an alias for your Scipion executable. During installation the plugin:

  1. Creates a Conda environment called hax (Python 3.11).
  2. Reads nvidia-smi to find the highest CUDA version your driver supports, and installs hax-em[cuda12] or hax-em[cuda13] into that environment.

If the installation stops with a CUDA error

The installer refuses to continue when nvidia-smi does not run, or when the driver only supports CUDA 11 or older. Check nvidia-smi in a terminal, update the driver to 525 or newer if needed, and launch the installation again.

Using an existing Hax environment

Protocols activate Hax with the command stored in the plugin variable HAX_ENV_ACTIVATION (default: conda activate hax). Set it in your Scipion configuration to point the plugin at a different environment.

docs.title: Finding the protocols
docs.text:
Open a project and switch the protocol panel on the left to the Flexibility Hub view. The Hax protocols are grouped as follows (you can also find any of them by name with the protocol search box):

Section Protocol (as shown in Scipion) Hax program Landscape estimation train - Zernike3Deep Zernike3Deep Landscape estimation flexible align - HetSIREN HetSIREN Landscape estimation predict - HetSIREN HetSIREN (--mode predict with a trained network) Landscape consensus train - FlexConsensus FlexConsensus Landscape consensus interactive consensus - FlexConsensus FlexConsensus (--mode predict) Data analysis filter latent space Filter Latents Data analysis annotate space Annotate Space Map reconstruction reconstruct MoDART MoDART Map reconstruction angular align - ReconSIREN ReconSIREN Gray level adjustment adjust gray scale - images Image Gray-Scale Adjustment Gray level adjustment adjust gray scale - volume Volume Gray-Scale Adjustment

Programs without a protocol

The following programs are only available from the command line or the Hax GUI:

  • Preprocess Particles and Preprocess Volumes. In Scipion, use the Downsample option of the HetSIREN and Zernike3Deep protocols, or a resize protocol from another package.
  • Reconstruct Volume. Any Scipion reconstruction protocol gives you the consensus map.
  • Estimate Latent Covariances and Latent Space Deconvolution.
  • Decode States from Latents. The landscape protocols already decode a set of states for you (see Outputs), and annotate space generates any other state you select.
  • Display Metrics, which is replaced by the TensorBoard viewer (see Viewers).

docs.title: What the plugin does for you
docs.text:
• Converts the inputs. The particle set, with its CTF and alignment, is written as Xmipp metadata, and the sampling rate is read from the set. Reference maps and masks are resized to the particle box when needed.
  • Downsamples on request. With Downsample the images before training? set to Yes (HetSIREN, Zernike3Deep), the particles, reference and mask are resized to the chosen box before training. ReconSIREN always works at the box set in Downsample particles to this box size. Output volumes are resampled back to the original box and shifts are rescaled to the original pixel size.
  • Trains and predicts in one run. The training protocols train the network and then run --mode predict on the same particles, so the latent space is available as soon as the run finishes. If you Continue a run whose network is already trained, training is skipped.
  • Uses one GPU per run. Hax protocols run on the first GPU ID given in the form.
  • Returns Scipion objects. Particles come back as Flexibility Hub particles carrying their latent vector, so any Flexibility Hub protocol (from Hax or another plugin) can use them.

docs.title: Form fields and command-line options
docs.text:
Most form fields correspond one to one to a command-line option, and their help texts follow the program pages. Fields marked as advanced only appear after you raise the expert level in the protocol form. A few fields deserve a note:

Form field Command-line option Note CTF correction type --ctf_type Same choices as on the Core Concepts page. Lazy loading into RAM --load_images_to_ram Yes loads every image into RAM; No memory-maps them. Path to SSD scratch folder --ssd_scratch_folder Only used when images are memory-mapped. Estimate batch size automatically? --batch_size auto Mass transportation (HetSIREN) --transport_mass Unlocks the decoder options of the Reconstruction tab. Fine tune previous network? (HetSIREN) --reload <previous run> Point it at an earlier flexible align - HetSIREN run. Reconstruction mode (MoDART) --reconstruct_halves Gold standard keeps the two unfiltered half maps. Correct motion blurred artifacts? (MoDART) --motion_correction <network> --poses_refined_by <network> Uses the network stored with the input particles. Their poses already include its refinement, so MoDART does not apply it twice. Refinement iterations (MoDART) --refine_iterations Fine-tunes that network with the parameters of its training run. It must have been trained on the particles at their original size (no downsampling).

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text: Protocol Outputs flexible align - HetSIREN outputParticles: the particles with their latent vector and the poses refined by the network. outputVolumes: 20 states decoded at k-means centres of the landscape. outputLearnedReference: only when the reference is learned (Learn reference epochs > 0). predict - HetSIREN outputParticles and outputVolumes, as above, for new particles. train - Zernike3Deep outputParticles and outputVolumes, as for HetSIREN. angular align - ReconSIREN outputParticles with the estimated poses, outputVolumes with the consensus map, and outputHetVolumes with the preliminary heterogeneous maps. train - FlexConsensus One particle set per input landscape, each with the consensus coordinates and the per-particle consensus and representation errors. interactive consensus - FlexConsensus The subset of particles you keep in the error histogram (see Viewers). filter latent space The particles that remain after removing landscape outliers. annotate space A set of classes and a set of volumes, one per selection you save in the viewer. reconstruct MoDART outputVolume: the FSC-filtered map. In Gold standard mode the half maps are attached to it. adjust gray scale - images outputParticles: the adjusted images, with the scale and offset applied to each one. adjust gray scale - volume outputVolume: the input volume multiplied by the fitted scale (at its own box, even if the particles have a different one).

docs.title: Viewers
docs.text:
• TensorBoard: available for the HetSIREN, Zernike3Deep, ReconSIREN, FlexConsensus and MoDART runs. Analyze the results of the run to open TensorBoard in your browser, with the same curves and images as Display Metrics. TensorBoard stops by itself when you close the browser tab.
  • FlexConsensus error histogram: analyze an interactive consensus - FlexConsensus run and choose the consensus or the representation error. Selecting a threshold on the histogram creates a new particle set with the particles below it.
  • Annotate Space: the annotate space protocol opens the Annotate Space window while it runs and waits for you. Save your selections, close the window, and the protocol turns them into classes and volumes.

Landscapes from other plugins

annotate space also accepts landscapes computed by other Flexibility Hub plugins (CryoDRGN, OPUS-DSD, DynaMight in RELION and 3D Flex in cryoSPARC) when those plugins are installed.

docs.title: A typical Scipion session
docs.text:
1. Bring in your data. Import the particles (or use the output of a refinement protocol from RELION, cryoSPARC or Xmipp) together with the consensus map and, optionally, a mask.
  2. No poses yet? Run angular align - ReconSIREN to estimate them and an initial map.
  3. Estimate the landscape with flexible align - HetSIREN or train - Zernike3Deep. Follow the training with the TensorBoard viewer.
  4. Clean or merge landscapes (optional). Run filter latent space to remove outliers, or train - FlexConsensus to compare the landscapes of several methods.
  5. Explore the landscape with annotate space and save the states you are interested in as classes.
  6. Reconstruct with reconstruct MoDART, either the whole set or the particles of a class. Set Correct motion blurred artifacts? to Yes when the particles come from HetSIREN (with mass transport) or Zernike3Deep.

For what happens at each stage, and how to choose between the programs, see Pipelines.

docs.title: Verify Your Installation
docs.text:
A quick way to confirm Hax is installed correctly is to list the programs:

hax_project_manager -h

If that prints the summary of programs, the package imports and the CLI works. To be sure the GPU stack (JAX, CUDA, cuML…) is actually working end to end, run the built-in test suite.

docs.title: The Hax test suite
docs.text:
Hax ships a suite of fast, data-free smoke tests. They generate a small synthetic phantom with built-in conformational heterogeneity (a different conformation, pose, shift and CTF per particle) and then drive every program through its real CLI across a broad sweep of options. If your installation is healthy, everything passes; if something in the GPU stack is broken, you get a clear failure pointing at the program and scenario that broke.

No real data required

The phantom is created on the fly, so you do not need any of your own particles to run these tests — they are purely a check that the software runs.

docs.title: Get the tests
docs.text:
The tests live in the tests/ folder of the source repository and are not included in the PyPI package, so grab them from GitHub:

git clone https://github.com/DavidHerreros/hax-em.git
cd hax-em

If you already installed Hax from a clone, you can simply cd into that clone instead.

docs.title: Run them
docs.text:
Run the suite with the Python of the environment where hax-em is installed (the same interpreter is used to spawn the CLI subprocesses):

# Run the whole suite on GPU 0
python tests/run_tests.py --gpu 0 all

You can also test a single program, or skip the slower scenarios:

# Just one program
python tests/run_tests.py --gpu 0 hetsiren

# Skip slow cases (those that fit Gaussians to a volume)
python tests/run_tests.py --gpu 0 --quick all

A successful run ends with:

ALL TESTS PASSED

If anything fails, it ends with SOME TESTS FAILED and a non-zero exit code, and the offending program/scenario is marked FAIL in the output.

docs.title: Useful options
docs.text: Option Purpose --gpu <id> GPU to use for the runs (sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES). --quick Skip slow scenarios (e.g. those needing the Gaussian volume fit). --keep Keep the temporary work directory afterwards so you can inspect outputs. --workdir <path> Put the phantom data and run outputs in a specific folder. --python <exe> Use a specific Python interpreter to spawn the CLI subprocesses.

docs.title: What is covered
docs.text:
The suite drives the following programs through their CLIs:

preprocess_particles, preprocess_volumes, hetsiren, reconsiren, reconsiren_het_only, zernike3deep, estimate_latent_covariances, latent_space_deconvolution, filter_latents, flexconsensus, decode_states_from_latents, modart, reconstruct_volume, annotate_space, image_gray_scale_adjustment, volume_gray_scale_adjustment, display_metrics.

Run python tests/run_tests.py --help to see the exact, up-to-date list for your version.

Most scenarios check that a program runs: it exits cleanly and writes the outputs it promised. The two preprocessing programs go further — because their contract is exact, their runs are followed by a verification step that reads the results back and checks the sampling rate, the rescaled in-plane shifts and the resized pixel data against values recomputed independently with NumPy. So a preprocess_particles run that quietly forgot to rescale the shifts would fail the suite, not pass it.

docs.title: Tips & troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Use the right environment. Run the suite inside the Conda environment where hax-em was installed, so JAX, cuML and the other GPU dependencies resolve correctly.
  • The phantom is built on the CPU. The runner generates data on the CPU (so it holds no GPU memory) and only the program subprocesses use the GPU you select with --gpu.

  • Inspect a failure. Re-run just the failing program with --keep to retain its work directory, then look at the produced files and logs:

    python tests/run_tests.py --gpu 0 --keep hetsiren

  • Out of GPU memory during tests? This usually mirrors a real run — make sure no other process is using the GPU (nvidia-smi).

  • A failing suite right after installation most often points to a driver/CUDA mismatch — revisit the installation requirements (NVIDIA driver ≥ 525, matching CUDA extra).

docs.title: Programs Overview
docs.text:
Hax bundles sixteen command-line programs, all launched through hax_project_manager (see The Command Line). They fall into seven families, listed below in roughly the order you would use them in a project.

Every program page follows the same layout

What it does → reference paper → when to use it → parameters → example commands → outputs → tips. If a term is unfamiliar, check Core Concepts first.

docs.title: Preprocessing
docs.text:
Optional, but often the first thing you run: shrink the box to trade resolution for speed and VRAM, and correct the CTF once instead of every epoch.

  • Preprocess Particles

    Resize/crop a particle stack and optionally Wiener- or phase-flip-correct it.

    Preprocess Particles

  • Preprocess Volumes

    Resize/crop reference maps and masks to match a preprocessed particle set.

    Preprocess Volumes

docs.title: Heterogeneity analysis
docs.text:
The core of Hax: learn how your molecule moves and place every particle on a conformational landscape.

  • HetSIREN

    Real-space heterogeneous reconstruction, refinement and disentanglement of conformational states.

    HetSIREN

  • Zernike3Deep

    Deep-learning estimation of continuous motions using the 3D Zernike basis.

    Zernike3Deep

  • ReconSIREN

    Ab initio pose/shift assignment and initial volume estimation.

    ReconSIREN

docs.title: Consensus & deconvolution
docs.text:
Combine and refine landscapes coming from one or several methods.

  • FlexConsensus

    Merge multiple conformational landscapes into one consensus space.

    FlexConsensus

  • Estimate Latent Covariances

    Estimate the per-particle uncertainty needed for landscape deconvolution.

    Estimate Latent Covariances

  • Latent Space Deconvolution

    Sharpen a landscape by removing the blurring caused by estimation noise.

    Latent Space Deconvolution

docs.title: Gray-scale adjustment
docs.text:
Match intensity levels between maps and images before further analysis.

  • Image Gray-Scale Adjustment

    Even out the contrast of the particles against the projections of a map (closed form).

    Image Gray-Scale Adjustment

  • Volume Gray-Scale Adjustment

    Put a map on the gray scale of a set of particles (closed form).

    Volume Gray-Scale Adjustment

docs.title: Latent post-processing
docs.text:
Utilities to turn latent spaces into volumes or to clean them up.

  • Decode States from Latents

    Generate 3D volumes from a trained network and a list of latent vectors.

    Decode States from Latents

  • Filter Latents

    Remove outliers from a latent space using z-scores.

    Filter Latents

docs.title: Reconstruction
docs.text:
• Reconstruct Volume

    Single-pass consensus map from posed particles, FSC-denoised and gray-scale calibrated.

    Reconstruct Volume

  • MoDART

    Least-squares reconstruction with motion-blur correction from deformation fields.

    MoDART

docs.title: Visualization
docs.text:
• Annotate Space

    Interactive landscape exploration with real-time volume generation.

    Annotate Space

  • Display Metrics

    Launch a TensorBoard dashboard to monitor training metrics.

    Display Metrics

docs.title: Annotate Space
docs.text:
At a glance

CLI name: annotate_space · Family: Visualization · Trains a network: no · Interface: interactive desktop GUI (PyQt5 + napari)

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
Annotate Space is an interactive viewer for your conformational landscape. Instead of staring at raw numbers, you see your latent space as a navigable point cloud: every point is a particle, and nearby points are similar conformations. You can lasso regions, cluster along any direction, and — when connected to a heterogeneity method — generate the 3D volume for any point in real time.

It is the natural place to explore a landscape after you have estimated it: find the distinct states, trace a motion, and export the conformations that matter.

When connected to ChimeraX (via --chimerax_binary), generated volumes can be displayed and morphed live as you move through the landscape.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: The interactive annotation of conformational landscapes is part of the Hax heterogeneity framework — see the HetSIREN and Zernike3Deep references on the Support page for the underlying methods that produce the landscapes you explore here.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• To explore a latent space produced by any Hax method (or by an external method, as long as you can save it as .txt/.npy).
  • To select conformational states or cluster the landscape.
  • To generate volumes on the fly from selected points (requires a connected method) or to browse pre-computed volumes.

docs.title: Modes of operation
docs.text:
• View only — just inspect the landscape (no volume generation). This is automatic when neither --env_name nor --volumes_path is provided, or you can force it with --only_view.
  • Pre-saved volumes — browse a fixed set of volumes you already computed (--volumes_path).
  • Live generation — generate volumes in real time from the heterogeneity method that produced the landscape (--env_name + --server_functions_path).

docs.title: Required
docs.text: Option Type Description --z_space path The latent space to display, saved as .txt or .npy. --path path Folder where the viewer's outputs (selections, generated volumes) are saved.

docs.title: Display
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --z_space_reduced path — A reduced-dimensionality version of the latent space (.txt/.npy) to display. If omitted, the original --z_space is shown. --only_view flag off Display only — disable state generation. Automatic when neither --env_name nor --volumes_path is given.

docs.title: Volume generation
docs.text:
Option Type Default Description --volumes_path path — A .txt file listing one volume path per landscape point, in the same order as the points. Lets you browse pre-saved conformations without a live method. --env_name str hax Name of the Conda environment where the heterogeneity software used to estimate the landscape is installed (for live generation). --server_functions_path path — Required with --env_name. A Python .py file defining a class with prepare_heterogeneity_program and decode_state_from_latent methods, so the viewer can drive the method to generate conformations. An example ships in the source at hax/viewers/server_loading_functions/load_model.py. --chimerax_binary path — Absolute path to the ChimeraX binary, to display/morph generated volumes in ChimeraX.

Custom parameters

The viewer also accepts arbitrary extra parameters of the form --my_parameter VALUE (number or string). These are passed through to your heterogeneity method and are useful in combination with --server_functions_path.

docs.title: Example commands
docs.text:
View only — just explore a landscape:

hax_project_manager annotate_space \
    --z_space results/latents.npy \
    --path annotation/ \
    --only_view

Browse pre-saved volumes along the landscape:

hax_project_manager annotate_space \
    --z_space results/latents.npy \
    --volumes_path decoded_states/volume_list.txt \
    --path annotation/

Live generation with ChimeraX display:

hax_project_manager annotate_space \
    --z_space results/latents.npy \
    --env_name hax \
    --server_functions_path my_loader.py \
    --chimerax_binary /opt/chimerax/bin/ChimeraX \
    --path annotation/

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
In --path:

  • selections_layers/ — your saved selections and the representative volumes you generated.
  • Any volumes generated during the session, plus related metrics.

docs.title: Tips & pitfalls
docs.text:
• Provide a --z_space_reduced (e.g. a 2D/3D UMAP of a high-dimensional space) for a clearer, plottable view while keeping the full space available.
  • For live generation, both --env_name and --server_functions_path are required; model the .py loader on the example in the package source.
  • This is a GUI program — run it on a machine with a display (or an X-forwarding / remote-desktop setup), not a headless batch node.
  • Need the volumes for --volumes_path? Generate them with Decode States from Latents.

docs.title: Decode States from Latents
docs.text:
At a glance

CLI name: decode_states_from_latents · Family: Latent post-processing · Trains a network: no

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
A conformational landscape tells you where each shape lives — but to see a shape you need to turn its latent vector back into a 3D volume. Decode States from Latents does exactly that: given a trained heterogeneity network (its decoder) and a list of latent vectors, it generates one 3D map per vector.

This is how you go from "interesting points on the map" to "volumes I can open in ChimeraX". The points can come from anywhere — cluster centres, a trajectory along a motion, the deconvolved landscape, or selections you made interactively.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• To materialize specific conformations selected from a landscape.
  • To generate a trajectory of volumes along a path through the latent space (a "movie" of the motion).
  • To export representative states for figures or further refinement.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Option Required Type Description --latents_file ✅ path File with the latent vectors to decode. Accepts .txt (NumPy text) or .npy (NumPy binary). One volume is produced per vector. --reload ✅ path Folder with a saved neural network — the network folder produced by a train run (e.g. zernike_run/Zernike3Deep or hetsiren_run/HetSIREN). --output_path ✅ path Folder where the decoded volumes are written.

docs.title: Example command
docs.text:
hax_project_manager --gpu 0 decode_states_from_latents \
    --latents_file selected_states.txt \
    --reload zernike_run/Zernike3Deep \
    --output_path decoded_states/

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
In --output_path, one volume per input vector:

decoded_volume_0000.mrc
decoded_volume_0001.mrc
decoded_volume_0002.mrc
...

The numbering follows the order of the vectors in --latents_file.

docs.title: Tips & pitfalls
docs.text:
• Point --reload at the network folder saved by a train run (e.g. zernike_run/Zernike3Deep).
  • The latent vectors must have the same dimensionality the network was trained with.
  • Latent vectors often come from Annotate Space selections, k-means cluster centres, or a deconvolved landscape.

docs.title: Display Metrics
docs.text:
At a glance

CLI name: display_metrics · Family: Visualization · Trains a network: no

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
Every Hax network writes its training progress — loss curves, validation curves and sample volume slices — into a metrics folder inside its --output_path. Display Metrics launches a TensorBoard dashboard pointed at one of those folders and opens it in your browser, so you can monitor a run while it trains or inspect it afterwards.

Watching these curves is the simplest way to tell whether training is healthy: a loss that steadily decreases and a validation curve that tracks it are good signs; a diverging or NaN-producing loss usually means the learning rate is too high (see Core Concepts).

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• To monitor a training run live.
  • To diagnose a run that failed or produced poor results.
  • To compare training and validation behaviour.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Option Required Type Description --logdir ✅ path Path to the TensorBoard log directory — i.e. the *_metrics/ folder a Hax program created inside its --output_path.

docs.title: Example command
docs.text:
hax_project_manager display_metrics \
    --logdir hetsiren_run/HetSIREN_metrics

The program prints the TensorBoard URL (typically http://localhost:6006) and opens it in a browser. It keeps running until you stop it with Ctrl+C.

docs.title: Tips & pitfalls
docs.text:
• The --logdir is the metrics folder, not the top-level output path. Examples:
    • HetSIREN_metrics/ (from HetSIREN)
    • Zernike3Deep_metrics/ (from Zernike3Deep)
    • ReconSIREN_metrics/, FlexConsensus_metrics/, MoDART_metrics/, …
  • You can launch it during training to watch progress in near real time.
  • Running on a remote server? Forward the TensorBoard port (e.g. ssh -L 6006:localhost:6006 user@server) to open the dashboard locally.

docs.title: Estimate Latent Covariances
docs.text:
At a glance

CLI name: estimate_latent_covariances · Family: Consensus & deconvolution · Trains a network: no

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
When a heterogeneity network assigns a latent vector to a particle, that estimate carries some uncertainty — a noisy particle could plausibly map to several nearby points on the landscape. This program measures that uncertainty, producing a covariance matrix for each particle's latent vector.

These covariances quantify how "smeared out" each point on the landscape is. They are the required input for Latent Space Deconvolution, which uses them to sharpen the landscape by removing that estimation blur.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
This tool supports the latent-space deconvolution workflow associated with the FlexConsensus framework:

Herreros, D., Perez Mata, C., Sanchez Sorzano, C.O. et al. Merging conformational landscapes in a single consensus space with the FlexConsensus algorithm. Nature Methods (2025). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41592-025-02841-w

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• Immediately before running Latent Space Deconvolution.
  • After training a heterogeneity network (HetSIREN, Zernike3Deep): just point this program at the saved network folder.

docs.title: Required
docs.text: Option Type Description --md path Metadata file with the images (plus alignments / CTF) needed to estimate the covariances — Xmipp .xmd, Relion .star, or CryoSPARC .cs (read directly). --output_path path Folder where the covariances and latents are saved.

docs.title: Optional
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --nn_path path — Folder containing a saved neural network (HetSIREN, Zernike3Deep…) — the network folder produced by a train run (e.g. zernike_run/Zernike3Deep). --batch_size int 64 Images processed on the GPU at once (GPU-memory lever). --load_images_to_ram flag off Load all images into RAM (fastest). Otherwise memory-mapped. --ssd_scratch_folder path — Fast-SSD folder used when memory-mapping.

docs.title: Example command
docs.text:
hax_project_manager --gpu 0 estimate_latent_covariances \
    --md particles.xmd \
    --nn_path zernike_run/Zernike3Deep \
    --batch_size 64 \
    --output_path covariances/

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
In --output_path:

  • covariance_matrices.npy — the stacked per-particle covariance matrices (shape ≈ [num_images, lat_dim, lat_dim]).
  • latents.npy — the latent vectors corresponding to those covariances.

Feed covariance_matrices.npy into Latent Space Deconvolution via its --covariances option.

docs.title: Tips & pitfalls
docs.text:
• Point --nn_path at the network folder saved by a train run (e.g. zernike_run/Zernike3Deep).
  • This program does not have a --mode option — it always performs covariance estimation.
  • The --md you pass should be the same particle set whose latents you want to deconvolve.

docs.title: Filter Latents
docs.text:
At a glance

CLI name: filter_latents · Family: Latent post-processing · Trains a network: no

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
Estimated landscapes often contain outliers — latent vectors that sit far from any dense region, usually corresponding to junk particles, misalignments, or noise. Filter Latents detects and removes them using a local z-score: for each vector it looks at how far it is from its nearest neighbours, and flags the ones that are unusually isolated.

The result is a cleaner latent space that gives more reliable clustering, exploration and reconstruction downstream.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• To clean a latent space before exploring or decoding it.
  • To obtain a list of good-particle indices you can apply to your metadata (use --return_ids).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Option Required Type Default Description --latents ✅ path — The .npy file with the latent space to filter. --output_path ✅ path — Folder where the filtered output is written. --thr float 1.0 Z-score threshold. Vectors more isolated than this are removed; lower values filter more aggressively. --n_neighbours int 10 Number of nearest neighbours used to compute each z-score. Smaller values are more sensitive to local structure. --return_ids flag off Return the indices of the kept vectors instead of the filtered vectors themselves. --batch_size int 1024 Vectors processed at once (GPU-memory lever).

docs.title: Example commands
docs.text:
Filter a latent space and keep the cleaned vectors:

hax_project_manager --gpu 0 filter_latents \
    --latents latents.npy \
    --thr 1.0 \
    --n_neighbours 10 \
    --output_path filtered/

Return the indices of the surviving particles (to subset your metadata yourself):

hax_project_manager --gpu 0 filter_latents \
    --latents latents.npy \
    --return_ids \
    --output_path filtered_ids/

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
In --output_path:

  • filtered_latents.npy — by default, the filtered latent vectors.
  • With --return_ids, the same file instead contains the integer indices of the vectors that passed the threshold.

docs.title: Tips & pitfalls
docs.text:
• Lower --thr to remove more aggressively; raise it to keep more.
  • Use a smaller --n_neighbours to capture fine local structure (e.g. small, tight clusters), or a larger one for a smoother global notion of outlier.
  • With --return_ids you keep full control: apply the indices to the original metadata to produce a cleaned particle set.

docs.title: FlexConsensus
docs.text:
At a glance

CLI name: flexconsensus · Family: Consensus & deconvolution · Trains a network: yes · Modes: train, predict

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
Different heterogeneity methods (Zernike3Deep, HetSIREN, cryoDRGN, 3DVA…) each produce their own latent space for the same particles — and those spaces are not directly comparable. FlexConsensus learns a single consensus latent space that reconciles all of them.

It is an autoencoder-style network: it takes the latent vectors that several methods assigned to the same, identically-ordered set of particles, and finds the common space that best agrees with all inputs. The result lets you compare methods on equal footing, identify which features are reproducible across methods, and obtain a more robust landscape than any single method alone.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: Herreros, D., Perez Mata, C., Sanchez Sorzano, C.O. et al. Merging conformational landscapes in a single consensus space with the FlexConsensus algorithm. Nature Methods (2025). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41592-025-02841-w

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• You ran several heterogeneity methods and want to merge their landscapes.
  • You want to validate a landscape by checking which features survive across methods.
  • You want a consensus space to drive downstream exploration or reconstruction.

docs.title: Input format
docs.text:
Each input space is a .npy file containing the latent vectors for all particles.

All inputs must be aligned and equal-length

Every input .npy must have the same number of elements, in the same order — the first vector in each file must correspond to the same particle, and so on. FlexConsensus relies on this one-to-one correspondence.

You may name each input using the NAME:path convention, which makes prediction much easier later:

--input_space Zernike:zernike.npy --input_space HetSIREN:hetsiren.npy

If you give just a path, inputs are auto-named Input_0, Input_1, … in command-line order.

docs.title: Required
docs.text: Option Type Description --input_space path(s) One or more .npy files with the input spaces to merge. Repeatable. Accepts either plain paths or the NAME:path form (recommended, especially for predict). All inputs must have the same number of elements, in the same order. --mode choice train or predict (predict needs --reload). --output_path path Folder where the trained network and consensus spaces are saved.

docs.title: Model & training
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --lat_dim int min input dim Dimensionality of the consensus latent space. Defaults to the smallest dimension among the inputs. --epochs int 100 Number of passes over the data. --batch_size int 1024 Vectors processed at once (latent vectors are small, so the batch can be large). --learning_rate float 1e-5 Step size of learning; lower ~10× if it diverges. --reload path — A previously trained FlexConsensus network, to fine-tune or to run predict.

docs.title: Example commands
docs.text:
Train a consensus from two methods' latent spaces:

hax_project_manager --gpu 0 flexconsensus \
    --input_space Zernike:zernike_latents.npy \
    --input_space HetSIREN:hetsiren_latents.npy \
    --mode train \
    --epochs 150 \
    --output_path flexconsensus_run/

Predict the consensus representation for those inputs:

hax_project_manager --gpu 0 flexconsensus \
    --input_space Zernike:zernike_latents.npy \
    --input_space HetSIREN:hetsiren_latents.npy \
    --mode predict \
    --reload flexconsensus_run/ \
    --output_path flexconsensus_predict/

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
After training:

  • FlexConsensus/ — the trained consensus network.
  • FlexConsensus_metrics/ — training curves (view with Display Metrics).

After predict, for each named input (e.g. Zernike):

  • Zernike_consensus.npy — that input mapped into the consensus space.
  • Zernike_consensus_error.npy — the consensus error per particle.
  • Zernike_representation_error.npy — how well the consensus represents that input.

The error files are useful for spotting particles or regions where the methods disagree.

docs.title: Tips & pitfalls
docs.text:
• The ordering and length of every input space must match exactly — re-export them from the same particle set if unsure.
  • Use the NAME:path form so the per-input output files are clearly labelled and easy to predict.
  • A consensus --lat_dim cannot exceed your smallest input space's dimensionality.

docs.title: HetSIREN
docs.text:
At a glance

CLI name: hetsiren · Family: Heterogeneity analysis · Trains a network: yes · Modes: train, predict

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
HetSIREN is a neural network that performs heterogeneous reconstruction directly in real space. Instead of producing one averaged map, it learns a conformational landscape — a compact description of how your molecule changes shape across the dataset — and can reconstruct, refine and even disentangle the different conformational states hidden in your particles.

In plain terms: you give HetSIREN your particle images (and, optionally, a reference volume), and it learns both what shapes are present and how to build the 3D map for any given shape. Because it works in real space, it can focus on a region of interest through a mask, and it can either keep the molecular mass fixed (pure reconstruction) or actively move the mass to model motion (the --transport_mass option).

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: Herreros, D., Mata, C.P., Noddings, C. et al. Real-space heterogeneous reconstruction, refinement, and disentanglement of CryoEM conformational states with HetSIREN. Nature Communications 16, 3751 (2025). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-59135-0

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• You want a flexible, high-fidelity heterogeneous reconstruction in real space.
  • You want to refine an existing consensus map towards the conformational states present in your data (provide it with --vol).
  • You want to study very local motions (consider --implicit_network with --transport_mass) or motions in a specific region (use a --mask, optionally with --local_reconstruction).
  • Your box size is large and you want to model motion by transporting mass (--transport_mass).
  • You have a sharper map of the same particles (e.g. a motion-corrected MoDART map) and want to fine-tune a trained network on it (--reload with --refit_reference).

It also handles tomography (subtomogram) data automatically: if the input metadata contains subtomo_labels, HetSIREN trains its TomoSIREN variant.

No reference map? In train mode, if neither --vol nor --mask is given, HetSIREN first reconstructs a consensus volume from the input poses and uses it as the reference.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: You can also pass any of these options through a YAML/JSON file with --config (see The Command Line).

docs.title: Required
docs.text: Option Type Description --md path Metadata file with the images (plus alignments / CTF) to analyze — Xmipp .xmd, Relion .star, or CryoSPARC .cs (read directly). If the metadata contains the label subtomo_labels, the tomography variant (TomoSIREN) is trained instead, and pose/CTF decoupling is handled for you. --sr float Sampling rate (pixel size) of the images/volume, in Å/px. --ctf_type choice How to handle the CTF: None, apply, wiener, precorrect or premultiplied (images that already carry one CTF multiplication, as in many tomography exports). See Core Concepts. --mode choice train or predict (predict needs --reload). --output_path path Folder where all results are saved.

docs.title: Inputs & region of interest
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --vol path — Reference volume. If given, HetSIREN learns to refine this volume towards the heterogeneous states in the images. If neither --vol nor --mask is given in train mode, a consensus volume is reconstructed from the input poses and used as the reference. --mask path auto Binary reconstruction mask. Should cover the volume where the motions of interest are expected to happen. If omitted, a spherical mask is used, or (with --transport_mass) a mask derived from the reference. --local_reconstruction flag off Switch to local heterogeneous reconstruction/refinement, restricted to the region enclosed by the reference mask. Requires a reference volume. Overrides --transport_mass. --transport_mass flag off Let HetSIREN move the mass inside the mask (learned displacements of the points) instead of reconstructing on a fixed lattice. When combined with a reference volume, use a tight mask covering the regions to analyze.

docs.title: Model configuration
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --lat_dim int 8 Dimensionality of the latent space (the "map of shapes"). Must be even: the latent is split into a motion half and an occupancy half. --num_gaussians int auto Number of Gaussians fitted to the reference volume before training. By default the count is grown until the fit reaches FSC ≥ 0.5 on every populated shell (see --fit_resolution); set it to fix the number yourself (e.g. to the number of residues). --fit_resolution float — Resolution (Å) the automatic Gaussian fit has to reproduce. --lattice_stride int 1 Keep one fixed-lattice point every this many voxels along each axis. Trades resolution for memory. --bilinear_scatter flag off Spread each fixed-lattice point over its four neighbouring pixels instead of the nearest one. --implicit_network flag off Use an implicit (coordinate-based) decoder: more accurate for very local motions, at a higher memory cost. Only with --transport_mass. --point_transformer flag off Use a point-transformer decoder on the Gaussian point cloud. Only with --transport_mass; ignored if --implicit_network is also set. --film_heads flag off Replace the implicit SIREN heads (and the point-transformer occupancy head) by a coordinate SIREN modulated by the latent through FiLM layers. --motion_only flag off Estimate conformational changes only: the amplitudes stay at their reference values. Only with --transport_mass. --encoder_arch choice convnn Encoder mapping each image to its latent: convnn (convolutional), mlpnn (MLP) or resmlp (residual MLP with LayerNorm on the Fourier-cropped image and a bounded latent). --train_inverse flag off Additionally train an inverse decoder mapping the deformed point cloud back to the latent. Only meaningful with --transport_mass (disabled otherwise). --denoising_strength float 1e-4 Weight of the L1 denoising on the decoded densities. Higher = stronger denoising, but too high can erode protein signal. Recommended range: 1e-4 to 0.1.

docs.title: Regularization
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --kl_lambda float 0.0 Weight of the VAE KL divergence towards a standard-normal prior. 0 disables the VAE and uses a deterministic latent. --kl_free_bits float 0.5 KL floor (nats per latent dimension) below which a dimension is not penalized, to avoid posterior collapse. 0 gives a plain KL. Only used when --kl_lambda > 0. --decoupling_lambda float 1e-4 Weight of the decoupling regularization encouraging the conformation latent to be invariant to pose and CTF. Increase for stronger decoupling; 0 to relax. --nested_dropout float 0.0 Nested dropout on the decoded latent: during training each sample keeps only its first k latent dimensions, with k drawn from a Geometric(p) distribution. This orders the dimensions by importance (PCA-like), so the first ones carry the dominant motions. Typical 0.1–0.5; 0 disables it. --noise_invariance_strength float 0.0 Penalizes latent dimensions that change when the noise changes: each image is encoded again with a second draw of noise, colored like the image background, and the loss is 1 − correlation between both latents, per dimension. After the first epoch its weight is recalibrated every epoch so its encoder gradient is this fraction of the reconstruction one. Typical 0.1–0.5; 0 disables it. Ignored for tomography data. --deformation_strength float 0.3 Strength of the graph deformation priors (relative edge strain + repulsion) with respect to the reconstruction loss. After the first epoch the prior weight is recalibrated every epoch so its gradient on the decoder is this fraction of the reconstruction gradient, so the same value behaves alike on every dataset. Lower for larger motions, higher for stiffer ones; 0 disables it. Only with --transport_mass and a reference. --distance_preservation_lambda float 1e-4 Weight of the local distance preservation between the deformed and the mean state. Higher = stiffer deformations. --occupancy_strength float 0.0 Weight of the occupancy prior on the per-particle amplitude change: an L1 shrinkage (stronger where the reference is empty) plus a graph total variation favouring spatially coherent occupancy, both relative to the mean reference density so the value means the same on every dataset. Requires --transport_mass and a reference; 0 disables it. --occupancy_warmup_epochs float 3.0 Epochs over which the per-particle amplitude change is ramped in, so motion is learned before occupancy. 0 disables the ramp. --rigid_drift_lambda float 1.0 Weight of the penalty on the rigid motion that the rigid gauge removes from the decoder displacement field. --geometric_lambda float 0.0 Weight of the geometric-correction loss on the decoder Jacobian (Gram determinant), pushing towards a locally volume-preserving latent-to-shape map. Expensive; 0 disables it.

docs.title: Pose refinement
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --pose_refine_reg float 0.1 Weight of the hinge penalizing pose refinements beyond --pose_refine_max_angle. 0 disables it. --pose_refine_max_angle float 8.0 Rotation (degrees) the pose refinement may apply freely; the excess is penalized with --pose_refine_reg. --shift_refine_reg float 0.1 Weight of the hinge penalizing shift refinements beyond --shift_refine_max. 0 disables it. --shift_refine_max float 4.0 Shift (pixels) the refinement may apply freely; the excess is penalized with --shift_refine_reg. --rigid_gauge choice core Remove the global rigid motion from the decoder output so pose errors go to the pose head. core: frame fitted on the least-moving points; mass: mass-weighted fit; off: diagnostic only. Without --transport_mass it requires a reference volume (otherwise it is disabled with a warning).

docs.title: Reference update
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --refit_reference flag off With --reload in train mode: fit the Gaussians to --vol (e.g. a MoDART map) and fine-tune the reloaded network on them. The architecture of the reloaded network is kept, and every weight whose shape still matches is reused. Needs --vol and a network trained with --transport_mass and an implicit or point-transformer decoder. --learn_reference_epochs int 0 Learn the positions of the reference Gaussians during the first N epochs, then freeze them. Every third epoch only the reference moves (the networks and the deformation prior are paused), and every three epochs it is re-centred on the mean deformed positions of the 100 least-deformed particles. The rest lengths of the deformation prior follow it. The distance moved is printed every epoch and the result is saved as learned_reference.mrc. Needs --transport_mass and an implicit decoder; 0 disables it. --reference_lr float auto Step size (Adam) of --learn_reference_epochs. Default: 2e-4 × √(batch_size / 128).

docs.title: Images & reconstruction loss
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --loss_type choice mse Reconstruction loss: mse in image space or frc (Fourier Ring Correlation). The point-transformer decoder always uses frc. --whiten_loss flag off Weight every Fourier ring of the reconstruction loss by the inverse of the residual power: unweighted for the first 10 epochs, then updated every epoch from a running average of the residual, keeping the overall loss scale. Only changes the mse loss. --normalize_images flag off Normalize each particle (zero mean, unit std in the background outside 0.375 × box) before the encoder, the losses and the contrast fit of the Gaussians. --particle_diameter float auto Particle diameter (Å), used as the background for --normalize_images and for the soft circular mask of the images. Default: the extent of the mask. --per_image_contrast choice off Fit one contrast scale per particle inside the reconstruction loss instead of relying on the global contrast fixed before training. relative: scales normalized to a unit batch mean; absolute: raw least-squares scale. --recon_split_final float 0.1 Amplitude-term weight w of the reconstruction loss, from the first step: w × L(learned amplitudes, frozen positions) + (1 − w) × L(reference amplitudes, learned positions). Only with --transport_mass.

docs.title: Training control
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --epochs int 50 Number of passes over the dataset (~50–100 for ≈100k particles). --batch_size int / auto 8 Images on the GPU at once — the main GPU-memory lever. auto estimates the largest batch that fits on your GPU (in predict, auto falls back to 8). --learning_rate float 1e-4 Step size of learning. Lower it ~10× if training diverges/produces NaNs. --dataset_split_fraction list 0.8,0.2 Train/validation split as train,val (must sum to 1). --lr_schedule flag off Linear warmup (first 10% of training) plus cosine-decay learning-rate schedule instead of a constant rate. --grad_clip_norm float 1.0 Global-norm gradient-clipping threshold. 0 disables clipping. --ema_decay float 0.0 Decay of the exponential moving average of the weights (typical: 0.999); the averaged weights are exported as the final model. 0 disables it. --reload path — A previously saved network, to fine-tune or to run predict. If a reference volume was used, this folder must contain both HetSIREN and Gaussian_volume_fitting subfolders. To fine-tune it on a new reference, add --refit_reference.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --log_images_every int 1 Epochs between the cheap TensorBoard logs (predicted images, central slices of the predicted volumes). 0 disables them. --log_landscape_every int 5 Epochs between the expensive logs (latent-space embedding, intermediate volumes, angular distribution plots). Raise it if logging dominates the training time on small datasets; 0 disables them. --log_checkpoint_every int 5 Epochs between the checkpoints used to resume an interrupted training. 0 disables them. --log_time_budget float 0.0 Maximum fraction of the wall clock that may be spent logging (e.g. 0.05); above it the expensive logs are skipped until training catches up. 0 disables the guard. --log_sync flag off Log on the training thread instead of a background thread (useful for debugging).

docs.title: Data loading
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --load_images_to_ram flag off Load all images into RAM (fastest; needs enough memory). Otherwise images are memory-mapped from disk. --ssd_scratch_folder path — When memory-mapping, a fast-SSD folder to read data from. Strongly recommended if not loading to RAM.

docs.title: Example commands
docs.text:
Train a heterogeneous reconstruction from particles, applying the CTF:

hax_project_manager --gpu 0 hetsiren \
    --md particles.xmd \
    --sr 1.5 \
    --ctf_type apply \
    --mode train \
    --lat_dim 8 \
    --epochs 80 \
    --output_path hetsiren_run/

Refine an existing map and focus on a region with a mask, modelling motion by transporting mass:

hax_project_manager --gpu 0 hetsiren \
    --md particles.xmd \
    --vol consensus.mrc \
    --mask tight_mask.mrc \
    --sr 1.5 \
    --ctf_type apply \
    --transport_mass \
    --mode train \
    --output_path hetsiren_refine/

Fine-tune on a new reference, e.g. the motion-corrected MoDART map reconstructed with the network above:

hax_project_manager --gpu 0 hetsiren \
    --md particles.xmd \
    --vol modart_run/modart_map.mrc \
    --sr 1.5 \
    --ctf_type apply \
    --transport_mass \
    --implicit_network \
    --mode train \
    --reload hetsiren_refine/ \
    --refit_reference \
    --epochs 30 \
    --output_path hetsiren_refit/

Predict the latent vectors of every particle with a trained network:

hax_project_manager --gpu 0 hetsiren \
    --md particles.xmd \
    --sr 1.5 \
    --ctf_type apply \
    --mode predict \
    --reload hetsiren_run/ \
    --output_path hetsiren_predict/

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
After training, --output_path contains, among others:

  • HetSIREN/ — the trained network.
  • HetSIREN_No_Inv/ — the network saved before the (optional) inverse-decoder stage of --train_inverse.
  • HetSIREN_metrics/ — training/validation curves and sample volume slices (view with Display Metrics).
  • Intermediate_volumes/ — volumes decoded at cluster centres of the latent space, written every --log_landscape_every epochs.
  • Gaussian_volume_fitting/, consensus_volume.mrc — the Gaussian fit of the reference used internally (with --refit_reference, the new fit of --vol).
  • learned_reference.mrc — the reference learned with --learn_reference_epochs.
  • consensus_reconstruction.mrc (and consensus_mask.mrc with --transport_mass) — the automatic reference, when neither --vol nor --mask was given.
  • HetSIREN_CHECKPOINT/ — an intermediate checkpoint for resuming (removed on clean completion).
  • run_config.json — the fully-resolved parameters of the run (reusable as a --config).

After predict:

  • predicted_latents.xmd / .star — your metadata enriched with the predicted latent vector (and refined pose) of every particle. This is the file you feed to Annotate Space, Filter Latents or FlexConsensus.

docs.title: Tips & pitfalls
docs.text:
• predict requires --reload. Train first, then point --reload at the training output.
  • --lat_dim must be even. An odd value stops the run before the Gaussian fit.
  • Out of GPU memory? Use --batch_size auto or lower --batch_size; without --transport_mass, --lattice_stride 2 also cuts memory.
  • For motions confined to one region, a good mask dramatically improves results; --local_reconstruction (with a reference volume) takes this further.
  • --implicit_network (with --transport_mass) is the most accurate option for subtle local motion, at a memory cost.
  • Large-amplitude motions held back (with --transport_mass)? Lower --deformation_strength (e.g. 0.1); raise it for stiffer, more regular motions. Use --motion_only if you only want conformational changes, not occupancy.
  • A deformation shared by all particles? With --transport_mass --implicit_network, --learn_reference_epochs lets the reference positions move during the first epochs, so that common deformation goes into the reference instead of into every particle's field.
  • Iterating with MoDART? Fine-tune the trained network on the new MoDART map with --reload and --refit_reference instead of training a new one from scratch: the fine-tune keeps what the first network learned.
  • Latent space looks like a featureless ball? Combine --nested_dropout with --noise_invariance_strength (e.g. 0.1–0.5 each): dimensions that only fit noise are penalized and the remaining ones are ordered by importance, so the conformational variability concentrates in the first few dimensions. The current noise-invariance loss and weight are shown in the progress bar (noise_inv=loss/weight) and logged as Noise invariance (HetSIREN) in the training metrics.

docs.title: Image Gray-Scale Adjustment
docs.text:
At a glance

CLI name: image_gray_scale_adjustment · Family: Gray-scale adjustment · Trains a network: no · Modes: none (a single pass over the particles)

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
