The contrast of the particles in a data set is not uniform: ice thickness, defocus and dose make some images brighter or darker than others. Image Gray-Scale Adjustment measures that contrast for every particle and corrects it.

Each image is compared with the reference volume projected at the particle's pose, with its shift and CTF applied. The gray scale of the image (and, optionally, an offset) is the least-squares fit of the image to that projection, solved in closed form — the same per-image contrast fit HetSIREN uses during training. The images are then rescaled and written as a new stack.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• Before a heterogeneity analysis, so that differences in contrast between particles are not mistaken for differences in density.
  • To put the particles on the gray scale of a reference map (--per_image_contrast absolute).

docs.title: Required
docs.text: Option Type Description --md path Metadata file with the images, their poses and CTF — Xmipp .xmd, Relion .star, or CryoSPARC .cs (read directly). --vol path Reference volume. It must have the same box and sampling rate as the images. --sr float Sampling rate (pixel size), in Å/px. --ctf_type choice None, apply, wiener, precorrect or premultiplied (see below). --output_path path Folder where results are saved (created if needed).

docs.title: Adjustment
docs.text:
Option Type Default Description --per_image_contrast choice relative relative: each image is divided by its gray scale relative to the mean of the data set, so the contrast becomes even while the overall gray level is kept. absolute: each image is divided by its own gray scale, which puts every particle on the gray scale of the reference volume. --fit_offset flag off Also fit and subtract an offset per image (image = scale × projection + offset). By default only the scale is fitted, which assumes images normalized to a zero-mean background. --mask path — Binary mask of the region to match. The fit then only uses the pixels inside the projection of the mask. Without it, the whole image is used.

--ctf_type says what the stored images contain: apply, wiener and precorrect all mean raw images that carry their CTF, so the CTF is applied to the projections; premultiplied means the images were already multiplied by their CTF; None means they carry no CTF at all.

docs.title: Data loading
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --batch_size int 256 Images read and projected at once. Lower it if the GPU runs out of memory; it does not change the result. --threads int 8 Reader threads feeding the GPU. On a spinning disk, 1 or 2 can be faster. --ssd_scratch_folder path — Fast-disk folder where the images are cached (as float16) and read from — the same cache the other Hax programs build there.

docs.title: Example command
docs.text:
hax_project_manager --gpu 0 image_gray_scale_adjustment \
    --md particles.xmd \
    --vol reference.mrc \
    --sr 1.5 \
    --ctf_type apply \
    --output_path img_adjust/

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
• adjusted_images.mrcs — the adjusted image stack.
  • adjusted_images.<ext> — a copy of the input metadata pointing at the adjusted images, with two new columns, adjustment_a and adjustment_b: each adjusted image is adjustment_a × image + adjustment_b.

docs.title: Tips & pitfalls
docs.text:
• The fit needs reliable poses and the right CTF type. If most images come out anti-correlated with the projections, the program stops: check that the images and the volume have the same contrast (protein white) and that --ctf_type matches the data.
  • Images whose projection explains nothing (empty or badly aligned particles) are not amplified into noise: they get the median scale, and every scale is kept within 5× of the median. The program reports how many images this affected.
  • Up to a box of 256 px the projections are computed from a 2× oversampled transform, which keeps the fitted scales accurate to about 1%; above that size they are computed without oversampling to save memory, and are slightly less accurate.
  • See also Volume Gray-Scale Adjustment, which fits one scale for the volume instead.

docs.title: Latent Space Deconvolution
docs.text:
At a glance

CLI name: latent_space_deconvolution · Family: Consensus & deconvolution · Trains a network: yes · Modes: train, predict

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
A conformational landscape estimated from noisy particles is always slightly blurred: each true conformation gets spread out because the latent vector of every particle is uncertain. Latent Space Deconvolution removes that blur, producing a sharper, more faithful landscape in which distinct conformational states are easier to separate.

It uses the per-particle uncertainty measured by Estimate Latent Covariances to "undo" the smearing, much like deconvolving a blurred photograph once you know the blur kernel. The latent vectors of your images are recovered on the fly from the trained heterogeneity network you point it at.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: Herreros, D., Perez Mata, C., Sanchez Sorzano, C.O. et al. Merging conformational landscapes in a single consensus space with the FlexConsensus algorithm. Nature Methods (2025). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41592-025-02841-w

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• After Estimate Latent Covariances, to obtain a cleaner landscape before exploring it or decoding states from it.
  • When distinct conformations appear overlapping or smeared in your latent space.

docs.title: Required
docs.text: Option Type Description --md path Metadata file with the images — Xmipp .xmd, Relion .star, or CryoSPARC .cs (read directly). Their latent vectors are recovered on the fly from --nn_path and then deconvolved. --nn_path path Folder with a saved neural network (HetSIREN, Zernike3Deep…); its encoder recovers the latent vectors on the fly. --covariances path The .npy covariance file produced by Estimate Latent Covariances. --mode choice train or predict (predict needs --reload). --output_path path Folder where results are saved.

docs.title: Model & training
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --lat_dim int 3 Dimensionality of the deconvolution network's latent space. --deconvolution_strength float 1.0 How aggressively to deconvolve. 1.0 matches the blur implied by the covariances; larger values deconvolve more strongly, smaller values are more conservative. --epochs int 100 Number of passes over the data. --batch_size int 1024 Vectors processed at once. --reload path — A previously trained deconvolution network, to fine-tune or to run predict.

docs.title: Data loading
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --load_images_to_ram flag off Load all images into RAM (fastest). Otherwise memory-mapped. --ssd_scratch_folder path — Fast-SSD folder used when memory-mapping (defaults to the output path otherwise).

docs.title: Example commands
docs.text:
Train the deconvolution from a network and its covariances:

hax_project_manager --gpu 0 latent_space_deconvolution \
    --md particles.xmd \
    --nn_path zernike_run/Zernike3Deep \
    --covariances covariances/covariance_matrices.npy \
    --lat_dim 3 \
    --deconvolution_strength 1.0 \
    --mode train \
    --output_path deconv_run/

Predict the deconvolved latents:

hax_project_manager --gpu 0 latent_space_deconvolution \
    --md particles.xmd \
    --nn_path zernike_run/Zernike3Deep \
    --covariances covariances/covariance_matrices.npy \
    --mode predict \
    --reload deconv_run/ \
    --output_path deconv_predict/

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
• After train: deconvolver/ — the trained deconvolution network.
  • After predict: latents_deconvolved.npy — the sharpened latent space, ready for Annotate Space or Decode States from Latents.

docs.title: Tips & pitfalls
docs.text:
• Run Estimate Latent Covariances first — its output is a required input here.
  • Start with --deconvolution_strength 1.0. Increase it if states still overlap; decrease it if the landscape starts to look fragmented or artefactual.
  • A small --lat_dim (the default 3) gives a landscape you can plot and explore directly.

docs.title: MoDART
docs.text:
At a glance

CLI name: modart · Family: Reconstruction · Trains a reusable network: no (solves a least-squares reconstruction by conjugate gradient)

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
Flexible molecules produce motion-blurred reconstructions: because every particle is in a slightly different shape, averaging them smears the moving regions. MoDART is a real-space reconstruction algorithm that can correct for that motion blur using a deformation field learned by a heterogeneity network.

MoDART looks for the map whose projections best match the particle images, through each particle's pose and CTF. It solves this least-squares problem with a preconditioned conjugate gradient, one pass over the particles per iteration (--iterations).

Run on its own, MoDART produces a standard reconstruction. When you also supply a trained motion model via --motion_correction, it encodes every particle once with that network and, in every pass, warps the voxels with the particle's deformation field before projecting them. It also applies the pose refinement estimated by the network. The flexible regions then add up in the reference conformation instead of being blurred.

Two half maps (even/odd particles) are always reconstructed. Their FSC weights their average, so modart_map.mrc comes out filtered to the resolution the data support.

docs.title: Iterative refinement
docs.text:
A motion model is only as good as the reference it was trained on, and the motion-corrected map is usually sharper than that reference. With --refine_iterations N, MoDART closes the loop by itself. Each iteration:

  1. reconstructs a motion-corrected map with the current network;
  2. fine-tunes the network on that map, with the parameters of its original training plus the map as --vol, --reload and --refit_reference.

After the last iteration, a final map is reconstructed with the refined network. Every step runs as its own process, so each one gets the whole GPU.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: Herreros, D., Kiska, J., Ramirez-Aportela, E. et al. ZART: A Novel Multiresolution Reconstruction Algorithm with Motion-blur Correction for Single Particle Analysis. Journal of Molecular Biology 435, 168088 (2023). https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmb.2023.168088

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• To reconstruct a volume after a heterogeneity analysis, removing motion-induced blur.
  • To get half-maps and a half-map FSC for resolution estimation (--reconstruct_halves keeps the half maps).
  • To get a sharp map that accounts for the flexibility you modelled with HetSIREN (with transport of mass) or Zernike3Deep.
  • To improve the motion model and the map together: --refine_iterations alternates MoDART maps and fine-tunes of the network on them.

docs.title: Required
docs.text: Option Type Description --md path Metadata file with the images (plus alignments / CTF) — Xmipp .xmd, Relion .star, or CryoSPARC .cs (read directly). --sr float Sampling rate (pixel size), in Å/px. --ctf_type choice None, apply, wiener (treated as apply: the least-squares model already inverts the CTF), or precorrect. --output_path path Folder where results are saved.

docs.title: Reconstruction configuration
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --vol path — Starting map. Its contrast is first matched to the images (median of the per-image least-squares scales). Without it, the reconstruction starts from an empty map. --mask path auto Binary mask with the voxels to reconstruct. If omitted, it is derived from --vol, or from a consensus reconstruction of the particles. Must be binary. --symmetry_group str c1 Point-group symmetry: every particle is also used through each symmetry operator. Only c* and d* groups are supported. --reconstruct_halves flag off Also write the two unfiltered half-maps (even/odd particles). They are always reconstructed: their FSC filters the final map.

docs.title: Motion correction
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --motion_correction path(s) — Path to a trained HetSIREN (with transport of mass) or Zernike3Deep network (the HetSIREN / Zernike3Deep folder). When given, each particle's deformation field and refined pose are used in the reconstruction; otherwise a standard reconstruction is performed. Two paths (gold standard): the first network moves the even particles (first half), the second the odd ones. --field_smoothing float 0.0 Width, in Å, of a local-linear Gaussian smoothing of each particle's motion field. It removes non-rigid jitter while keeping rigid (and affine) motions exact. 0 disables it. --poses_refined_by path — Network whose pose refinement the input poses already include (e.g. the particles written by its predict). MoDART removes it before applying the refinement of --motion_correction, so it is not applied twice. --remove_mean_field flag off Subtract each network's particle-average motion field, so the map is reconstructed in the frame of the network's reference. It removes a static deformation the network may learn (e.g. to sharpen a blurred reference by moving its points), which otherwise distorts the map.

docs.title: Refinement
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --refine_iterations int 0 Number of refinement iterations (map, then fine-tune of the network on it). Needs a single --motion_correction network trained on all the particles. 0 disables it. --refine_epochs int training's Epochs of each fine-tune. By default, the ones of the network's training. --refine_learning_rate float training's Learning rate of the fine-tunes. By default, the one of the network's training. --refine_batch_size int / auto training's Batch size of the fine-tunes. By default, the one of the network's training. --refine_config path auto run_config.json of the network's training, whose parameters the fine-tunes reuse. By default, the one next to the network folder (written by the training in its --output_path).

docs.title: Solver
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --iterations int 10 Conjugate gradient iterations, one pass over the particles each. More iterations recover finer detail and also fit more noise. --regularization float 0.0 Tikhonov weight, relative to the mean diagonal of the normal equations.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --batch_size int 8 Images processed at a time (auto uses 8). It changes speed and GPU memory, not the result. With symmetry, each image counts once per symmetry operator. --chunk_size int 65536 Voxels projected at a time. Lower it if the GPU runs out of memory; it does not change the result. --load_images_to_ram flag off Load all images into RAM (fastest). Otherwise memory-mapped. --ssd_scratch_folder path — Fast-SSD folder used when memory-mapping.

docs.title: Example commands
docs.text:
Standard reconstruction (no motion correction):

hax_project_manager --gpu 0 modart \
    --md particles.xmd \
    --sr 1.5 \
    --ctf_type apply \
    --output_path modart_run/

Motion-corrected reconstruction using a trained Zernike3Deep model, keeping the half-maps:

hax_project_manager --gpu 0 modart \
    --md particles.xmd \
    --sr 1.5 \
    --ctf_type apply \
    --motion_correction zernike_run/Zernike3Deep \
    --reconstruct_halves \
    --output_path modart_motion/

Iterative refinement of a HetSIREN network (transport of mass, implicit decoder) and its map, three iterations:

hax_project_manager --gpu 0 modart \
    --md particles.xmd \
    --sr 1.5 \
    --ctf_type apply \
    --motion_correction hetsiren_run/HetSIREN \
    --refine_iterations 3 \
    --output_path modart_refined/

The fine-tunes read the training parameters from hetsiren_run/run_config.json.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
In --output_path:

  • modart_map.mrc — the average of the two half maps, weighted per shell by √(2·FSC / (1 + FSC)). During the run, modart_map_intermediate.mrc (and the intermediate half maps with --reconstruct_halves) is rewritten after every iteration and removed at the end.
  • modart_first_half.mrc, modart_second_half.mrc — the unfiltered half-maps, when --reconstruct_halves is used.
  • half_map_fsc.txt — the half-map FSC (columns 1/A and FSC), corrected for the mask by phase randomisation. The resolution at FSC = 0.143 is printed at the end of the run.
  • consensus_mask.mrc — the mask derived when no --mask is given, plus consensus_reconstruction.mrc when there is no --vol either.
  • MoDART_metrics/ — TensorBoard logs (relative residual of every iteration), viewable with Display Metrics.

With --refine_iterations, the files above come from the final map (made with the refined network), and each iteration N leaves:

  • iteration_N/modart/ — the MoDART run of that iteration (same files as above).
  • iteration_N/hetsiren/ or iteration_N/zernike3deep/ — the fine-tune of the network on that map. The refined network is the HetSIREN / Zernike3Deep folder inside it.

docs.title: Tips & pitfalls
docs.text:
• For motion correction, the model at --motion_correction must be a HetSIREN trained with transport of mass or a Zernike3Deep network — these are the ones that carry a deformation field.
  • With --motion_correction, pass the metadata with the poses the network was trained on. MoDART applies the network's pose refinement on top of them, so the predicted_latents metadata of a predict run, whose poses already include that refinement, would refine them twice. With such metadata, add --poses_refined_by <network>: MoDART then removes that refinement first.
  • --refine_iterations needs the network folder as the training wrote it (<output_path>/HetSIREN or <output_path>/Zernike3Deep) and its run_config.json (next to it, or given with --refine_config). A HetSIREN must have been trained with transport of mass and an implicit or point transformer decoder, which --refit_reference requires.
  • The fine-tunes take the MoDART map as --vol of the network's training, so run MoDART on particles with the same box and pixel size as that training (not the full-size particles of a network trained on downsampled ones).
  • Each iteration costs a MoDART run plus a fine-tune, by default as long as the original training (same --epochs). --refine_epochs shortens the fine-tunes. Epoch-based schedules of the training (e.g. --learn_reference_epochs) still apply to each of them.
  • Any --mask you pass must be binary.
  • Out of GPU memory? Lower --batch_size or --chunk_size; neither changes the result.

docs.title: Preprocess Particles
docs.text:
At a glance

CLI name: preprocess_particles · Family: Preprocessing · Trains a network: no

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
Preprocess Particles rewrites a particle stack into a smaller, optionally CTF-corrected one, and writes an updated metadata file to go with it.

Running a heterogeneity network on a smaller box is the single cheapest way to cut GPU memory and training time. Halving the box size divides the number of pixels — and roughly the memory a network needs — by four, at the cost of resolution: the new Nyquist frequency becomes 2 × sr × box_in / box_out Å. Doing that conversion once, up front, is much cheaper than making every downstream run resize on the fly.

The program applies up to three steps, in this order:

  1. Crop (--crop_box_size) — a real-space centred crop. It trims the field of view; the sampling rate is untouched, and so are the in-plane shifts.
  2. Resize (--new_box_size) — a Fourier crop/pad. It changes the sampling rate, so the in-plane shifts stored in the metadata are rescaled to match the new pixel size.
  3. CTF correction (--ctf_correction) — Wiener deconvolution or phase flipping.

Why the CTF step comes last

A CTF filter is diagonal in Fourier space, so it commutes with the spectral truncation that Fourier cropping performs. Correcting the CTF on the already-small box gives the same result on the retained band as correcting on the full box would, using a much cheaper FFT. The CTF oscillations beyond the new Nyquist frequency are exactly the ones the resize discards anyway.

Reading, computing and writing are overlapped: threads read batches ahead of the GPU, the GPU processes one batch at a time, and more threads stream the results into a memory-mapped output stack. Peak memory therefore scales with --batch_size, not with the number of particles — a 10⁶-particle stack costs about as much RAM as a 10⁴-particle one.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• To fit a bigger job on a smaller GPU, or to make a long training run finish sooner, when you do not need the highest-resolution detail.
  • To trim a generously padded box down to the particle (--crop_box_size) before downsampling.
  • To hand the networks CTF-corrected images once, instead of correcting them every epoch.

docs.title: Required
docs.text: Option Type Description --md path Metadata with the images (plus alignments / CTF) — Xmipp .xmd, Relion .star, or CryoSPARC .cs. --sr float Sampling rate of the input images, in Å/px. --output_path path Folder where the new stack and metadata are written.

docs.title: Box geometry
docs.text:
Option Type Default Description --crop_box_size int — Real-space centred crop, applied first. Trims the field of view at the original sampling rate. A value larger than the input box zero-pads instead. --new_box_size int — Box size after Fourier resizing, applied after the crop. This is the parameter that trades resolution for speed and VRAM.

Both must be even: hax evaluates CTFs on a zero-padded box, and an odd size would make the padded spectrum and the CTF grid disagree.

docs.title: CTF correction
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --ctf_correction choice none none, wiener (regularized CTF inversion — amplitudes and phases), or phase_flip (phases only). --wiener_epsilon float — Fixed Wiener regularization constant. Omit it to use the adaptive, per-image and frequency-dependent regularizer estimated from each image's spectral SNR — the recommended behaviour.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --batch_size int | auto 1024 Images processed at once. The CTF steps zero-pad each image by a factor of 2, so device memory scales with batch_size × (2 × box_out)². Pass auto to let hax pick the largest batch that fits — see below. --device choice auto auto (GPU when one is visible, else CPU), gpu, or cpu. --num_read_workers int 8 Threads reading batches from disk ahead of the device. Raise on a slow or networked filesystem. --num_write_workers int 4 Threads streaming processed batches into the output stack.

docs.title: --batch_size auto
docs.text:
auto compiles the kernel ahead of time at two batch sizes, reads XLA's own memory accounting, fits the (affine) peak-memory-vs-batch line, and solves for the largest batch that stays inside a 60 % slice of your GPU's memory — capped at 2048. Nothing is executed and no image data is allocated while probing, so it cannot itself OOM. On a CPU device, or any backend that does not report memory statistics, it prints a notice and falls back to 1024.

Use auto to make a big box fit, not to go faster

Unlike a training program, this one is bound by how fast images come off the disk, and the kernel's throughput is already flat above a batch of ~1024. auto therefore does not speed up a job that already fits — it adds a few seconds of extra compilation. What it does is prevent an out-of-memory crash on a large box.

On a 6 GiB card, a 512-box Wiener run at the default --batch_size 1024 tries to allocate 9 GiB and dies; auto selects 328 and completes. Conversely, at a 128-box the default already runs comfortably and auto merely picks the 2048 cap.

Reach for it when a run OOMs, or when you do not know how big a box your card can take. The chosen batch never changes the output — results are identical for any batch size.

docs.title: Output
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --relative_image_paths flag off Reference the stack by file name instead of absolute path, making the output folder relocatable. See the pitfall below.

docs.title: Example commands
docs.text:
Halve the box to fit a large dataset on a smaller GPU:

hax_project_manager --gpu 0 preprocess_particles \
    --md particles.xmd \
    --sr 1.5 \
    --new_box_size 128 \
    --output_path 00_preprocessed/

Trim a padded box, then downsample, and Wiener-correct the result:

hax_project_manager --gpu 0 preprocess_particles \
    --md particles.xmd \
    --sr 1.5 \
    --crop_box_size 192 \
    --new_box_size 96 \
    --ctf_correction wiener \
    --output_path 00_preprocessed/

The program prints the new sampling rate, which you pass to every downstream program:

     box            : 256 -> crop 192 -> resize 96
     sampling rate  : 1.5000 -> 3.0000 A/px   (Nyquist 3.00 -> 6.00 A)
     in-plane shifts: rescaled by 0.5000

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
In --output_path:

  • preprocessed_particles.mrcs — the new stack, with the new sampling rate in its header.
  • preprocessed_particles.xmd (or .star, matching the input extension) — metadata pointing at the new stack, with rescaled in-plane shifts. CTF columns, angles and labels are carried over untouched.
  • run_config.json — the fully-resolved parameters, reusable as a --config.

docs.title: Tips & pitfalls
docs.text:
• Pass the new --sr downstream. The program prints it; it is sr × box_cropped / box_resized. Forgetting this silently mis-models the CTF in every later run.
  • If you correct the CTF here, run downstream programs with --ctf_type None. The images are already corrected, and correcting them twice will corrupt the analysis. The program warns you about this when it finishes.
  • Resize your reference volume and mask too, with the same settings, using Preprocess Volumes. A map and images with different box sizes will not align.
  • Pick the box from the resolution you need, not from the memory you have: the resized Nyquist is 2 × sr × box_in / box_out Å, and no downstream program can recover detail beyond it.
  • Crop wide enough. A centred crop keeps the box centre, so shifts stay valid — but a particle with a large in-plane shift can fall outside a tight crop.
  • Image paths are absolute by default, so the output metadata reads back from any working directory. Use --relative_image_paths if you need to move or share the output folder; then downstream programs must be launched from inside it (the GUI does this automatically).
  • The GPU is the right choice here and is used by default: over a stack of 10⁵–10⁶ images it beats a many-core CPU by roughly 4–9×, even counting the host↔device transfers. Force --device cpu only when the GPU is busy with another job.
  • If a run dies with RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED, pass --batch_size auto rather than guessing a smaller number. Peak device memory grows with batch_size × (2 × box_out)², so a big box needs a much smaller batch than a small one.
  • Host RAM stays bounded no matter how large the batch: the read-ahead window is capped in bytes, not in batches, so peak RSS tracks --batch_size rather than the particle count.

docs.title: Preprocess Volumes
docs.text:
At a glance

CLI name: preprocess_volumes · Family: Preprocessing · Trains a network: no

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
Preprocess Volumes crops and/or resizes volumes — reference maps, masks, initial models — so they match a particle set that has been through Preprocess Particles.

It is the companion of that program: whenever you resize particles, the volume handed to the same network has to be resized identically, or its projections will not line up with the images. Pass the map and its mask in one call so they cannot drift apart.

Two steps, in this order:

  1. Crop (--crop_box_size) — a real-space centred crop, trimming the field of view at the original sampling rate. This is how you remove the empty solvent padding around a map.
  2. Resize (--new_box_size) — a Fourier crop/pad, changing the sampling rate by box_cropped / box_resized.

Cropping first is both the cheaper order — the FFT then runs on a smaller cube — and the usual intent: trim the solvent, then downsample what is left.

This program runs on the CPU, deliberately

A GPU does the 3D transform a few times faster, but on the boxes volumes actually come in that is a sub-second saving on a job that handles a handful of files — while a large box (768³ and up) will exhaust a mid-range card's memory during the complex-valued 3D FFT. A multi-threaded CPU FFT keeps a 512³ resize under a second with no such cliff. The batched, 10⁶-image particle path is where the GPU actually pays off.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• Together with Preprocess Particles, to keep the reference volume, the mask and the images on one box size and one sampling rate.
  • To trim the solvent padding around a map without touching its sampling rate.
  • To bring a map from another package onto the box your particles use.

docs.title: Required
docs.text:
Option Type Description --vol path… One or more volumes. Pass several paths to process them all with the same settings — the way to keep a map and its mask consistent. --output_path path Folder where the preprocessed volumes are written.

At least one of --crop_box_size / --new_box_size must be given, or there is nothing to do.

docs.title: Box geometry
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --crop_box_size int — Real-space centred crop, applied first. A value larger than the input box zero-pads instead. --new_box_size int — Cube size after Fourier resizing, applied after the crop. Use the same value you gave preprocess_particles.

docs.title: Other
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --sr float header Sampling rate of the input volumes, in Å/px. Read from each volume's header when omitted. --num_workers int -1 Threads used by the CPU FFT (-1 uses every core).

docs.title: Example commands
docs.text:
Match a particle set that was downsampled to a 128 box:

hax_project_manager preprocess_volumes \
    --vol reference.mrc mask.mrc \
    --sr 1.5 \
    --new_box_size 128 \
    --output_path 00_preprocessed_volumes/

Trim the solvent, then downsample — the volume counterpart of the particle example:

hax_project_manager preprocess_volumes \
    --vol reference.mrc mask.mrc \
    --sr 1.5 \
    --crop_box_size 192 \
    --new_box_size 96 \
    --output_path 00_preprocessed_volumes/

     reference.mrc: (256, 256, 256) @ 1.5000 A/px -> (96, 96, 96) @ 3.0000 A/px
     mask.mrc:      (256, 256, 256) @ 1.5000 A/px -> (96, 96, 96) @ 3.0000 A/px

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
In --output_path, one file per input:

  • <name>_preprocessed.mrc — the processed volume, with the new sampling rate in its header. Gray levels are preserved, so a resized map keeps the density scale of the original.
  • run_config.json — the fully-resolved parameters, reusable as a --config.

docs.title: Tips & pitfalls
docs.text:
• Use exactly the same --crop_box_size and --new_box_size you gave the particles. The map and the images must end on the same box and the same sampling rate.
  • Resize the mask in the same call. Processing it separately invites a mismatch. Note that a Fourier resize is not binary-preserving: re-threshold the result if a program demands a strictly binary mask.
  • --new_box_size requires a cubic volume. Crop a non-cubic one to a cube first with --crop_box_size.
  • If a volume's header carries no sampling rate, pass --sr explicitly.
  • Do not pass a particle stack to --vol. A stack and a volume are both 3D arrays, so a stack of N N×N particles even looks cubic. When the MRC header marks the file as an image stack — as everything Hax writes does — the program refuses it and points you at Preprocess Particles. A stack written by older software may carry no such flag, and then nothing can distinguish it from a volume.
  • In the GUI, a run that writes exactly one volume can be wired straight into a downstream --vol input. A run that writes several (a map and a mask) deliberately offers no such connector — picking one for you would be a coin flip — so select the file with the path picker.

docs.title: ReconSIREN
docs.text:
At a glance

CLI name: reconsiren · Family: Heterogeneity analysis · Trains a network: yes · Modes: train, predict

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
ReconSIREN estimates the pose (orientation), shifts (centering) and an initial 3D volume of your particles — from scratch if needed (ab initio). It is the tool to reach for at the very start of a project, when you have particle images but no reliable angular assignment yet, or when you want to refine an existing assignment.

It can also produce a set of preliminary heterogeneous maps by clustering its internal latent space, giving you an early look at the conformational variability before committing to a full heterogeneity analysis with HetSIREN or Zernike3Deep.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
ReconSIREN is part of the SIREN-based real-space reconstruction framework introduced alongside HetSIREN:

Herreros, D., Mata, C.P., Noddings, C. et al. Real-space heterogeneous reconstruction, refinement, and disentanglement of CryoEM conformational states with HetSIREN. Nature Communications 16, 3751 (2025). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-59135-0

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• You need an ab initio orientation/shift assignment and an initial map.
  • You want to refine an existing assignment (use --refine_current_assignment).
  • You have a high-resolution reference (e.g. from an atomic model) and only need angles, not a new map (use --do_not_learn_volume).
  • Your particle has symmetry (--symmetry_group).

docs.title: Required
docs.text: Option Type Description --md path Metadata file with the images (plus alignments / CTF) — Xmipp .xmd, Relion .star, or CryoSPARC .cs (read directly). --sr float Sampling rate (pixel size), in Å/px. --ctf_type choice None, apply, wiener, or precorrect. --mode choice train or predict (predict needs --reload). --output_path path Folder where all results are saved.

docs.title: Reconstruction behavior
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --vol path — Starting volume to assign angles/shifts against (otherwise ab initio). --mask path — Binary reconstruction mask covering the region where the relevant signal/motion lives. --num_gaussians int auto When a reference volume (--vol) is given, the number of Gaussians used to recreate it before training. By default the count is chosen automatically for high fidelity; set it to fix the number yourself (e.g. to the number of residues). --do_not_learn_volume flag off Only learn an angular assignment with shifts — do not learn a map. Useful with a high-resolution reference that needs no refinement. --refine_current_assignment flag off Refine the angles/shifts already present in the metadata instead of finding them ab initio. --symmetry_group str c1 Point-group symmetry to consider. Only c* and d* groups are supported (lower-case). Even with symmetry set, a symmetry-broken c1 set of angles is learned, so the angles can be used directly in a downstream reconstruction/refinement.

docs.title: Pose search
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --num_components int 18 Number of candidate pose hypotheses the encoder proposes per image during the ab initio search: for each image it evaluates this many orientations (anchored on a spherical grid), renders a projection for each, and keeps the best match. Higher covers orientation space more densely and is more robust to local minima, but increases GPU memory and compute roughly linearly (the main driver of ReconSIREN's training footprint). Lower it to fit a smaller GPU at the cost of a coarser search. --do_not_use_anchor_rotations flag off By default the proposed poses are composed with a fixed set of anchor rotations spread over a spherical grid (one per hypothesis), biasing the ab initio search to cover orientation space more evenly. Provide this to disable that composition.

docs.title: Training control
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --epochs int 50 Passes over the dataset (~50–100 for ≈100k particles). --batch_size int 8 Images on the GPU at once (GPU-memory lever). --learning_rate float 1e-4 Step size of learning; lower ~10× if it diverges. --dataset_split_fraction list 0.8,0.2 Train/validation split (must sum to 1). --reload path — A saved network to fine-tune or to run predict.

docs.title: Data loading
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --load_images_to_ram flag off Load all images into RAM (fastest). Otherwise memory-mapped. --ssd_scratch_folder path — Fast-SSD folder used when memory-mapping.

docs.title: Example commands
docs.text:
Ab initio pose/shift assignment and initial volume:

hax_project_manager --gpu 0 reconsiren \
    --md particles.xmd \
    --sr 1.5 \
    --ctf_type apply \
    --mode train \
    --epochs 60 \
    --output_path reconsiren_run/

Refine an existing assignment, respecting C2 symmetry:

hax_project_manager --gpu 0 reconsiren \
    --md particles_aligned.xmd \
    --sr 1.5 \
    --ctf_type apply \
    --refine_current_assignment \
    --symmetry_group c2 \
    --mode train \
    --output_path reconsiren_refine/

Predict angles, shifts and heterogeneous maps with a trained network:

hax_project_manager --gpu 0 reconsiren \
    --md particles.xmd \
    --sr 1.5 \
    --ctf_type apply \
    --mode predict \
    --reload reconsiren_run/ \
    --output_path reconsiren_predict/

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
After training:

  • ReconSIREN/ — the trained network, plus ReconSIREN_metrics/ and a ReconSIREN_CHECKPOINT/ for resuming.
  • reconsiren_map.mrc — the consensus 3D reconstruction.
  • reconsiren_hetmap_*.mrc — preliminary heterogeneous maps (one per cluster).
  • volumeAdjustment/ — a gray-level adjustment network, when a reference volume was used.

After predict:

  • predicted_pose_shifts.xmd / .star — metadata with predicted angles, shifts and latent codes — ready for a downstream reconstruction or heterogeneity analysis.
  • reconsiren_map.mrc and a set of reconsiren_hetmap_*.mrc heterogeneous maps (obtained by k-means clustering of the latent codes).

docs.title: Tips & pitfalls
docs.text:
• For symmetric particles, set --symmetry_group (e.g. c2, d7) — note the requirement that it be lower-case and limited to c*/d*.
  • With a trustworthy high-resolution reference, --do_not_learn_volume saves time by solving only the alignment.
  • The output angles/shifts are in c1 even when symmetry is provided, so they slot directly into standard reconstruction/refinement pipelines.

docs.title: Reconstruct Volume
docs.text:
At a glance

CLI name: reconstruct_volume · Family: Reconstruction · Trains a network: no (a single, non-iterative pass over the particles)

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
Your particles already carry poses. That is all a consensus map needs: by the projection-slice theorem each image is a central slice of the molecule's 3D Fourier transform, so the map is recovered by inserting every CTF-weighted slice at its posed orientation and dividing by the accumulated CTF power. Reconstruct Volume does exactly that, in one streaming pass — no iteration, no refinement, no network — and reaches whatever resolution the data supports.

Three things come for free with that formulation:

  • It knows its own resolution. The particles are split into two independent halves, reconstructed separately, and the FSC between the half-maps is measured. The resolution at FSC = 0.143 is printed at the end of the run.
  • It denoises optimally. That half-map FSC is turned into the MMSE filter and applied to the combined map: shells that carry signal pass untouched (no resolution is thrown away), shells that are noise are driven to zero (none is kept).
  • It is on the gray scale of your images. The finished map is forward-projected at a subset of the real poses and least-squares scaled against the actual images, so re-projecting it reproduces their contrast and value range — which is what makes it usable as a reference for the programs downstream.

It can also derive a binary mask of the protein region from the map it just produced (--write_mask), which is the --mask the heterogeneity programs expect.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• You have poses but no map (or a map you don't trust) and need a consensus reference to start a heterogeneity analysis with.
  • To produce the reference volume + mask pair that HetSIREN, Zernike3Deep and MoDART take in --vol / --mask, once, so that every downstream run reuses the same reference instead of rebuilding it.
  • As a baseline to compare a flexible reconstruction against: this is the map you get when the heterogeneity is averaged away, so it shows you exactly which regions the flexible methods sharpen.

HetSIREN does this on its own

If you launch HetSIREN with neither --vol nor --mask, it runs this same reconstruction internally and writes consensus_reconstruction.mrc + consensus_mask.mrc into its output folder. Running reconstruct_volume separately is worth it when you want to inspect the reference before training, tune the mask, or share one reference across several runs.

docs.title: Required
docs.text: Option Type Description --md path Metadata file with the images and their alignments (plus CTF) — Xmipp .xmd, Relion .star, or CryoSPARC .cs. The poses are what makes the reconstruction possible, so this program cannot run on an unaligned set. --sr float Sampling rate (pixel size), in Å/px. --ctf_type choice None, apply, wiener, or precorrect. Only whether the images carry a CTF matters here: all modes except None mean they do. --output_path path Folder where the map (and mask) are written.

docs.title: Reconstruction
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --tau float 0.05 Wiener floor of the reconstruction quotient. A numerical regularizer only — it keeps the shells with little CTF power from blowing up; the resolution is set by the data, not by this. Raise it if the map looks noisy at high frequency, lower it if it looks over-smoothed. --no_denoise flag off Skip the half-map FSC denoising and write the raw map. You then get no resolution estimate either. --no_gray_scale_calibration flag off Skip the global gray-scale calibration and keep the raw amplitudes.

docs.title: Mask
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --write_mask flag off Also derive a binary mask of the protein region from the reconstructed map and write it as consensus_mask.mrc. --mask_threshold float 0.02 Fraction of the map's maximum above which a voxel counts as protein. Raise for a tighter mask, lower for a looser one. Only used with --write_mask. --mask_dilate int 2 How many voxels to grow the mask by, so that a deformation estimated later has somewhere to move the mass into. Only used with --write_mask.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
Option Type Default Description --batch_size int 1024 Images read and inserted at once. The images are read on a thread pool while the GPU accumulates, so peak RAM tracks this value, not the number of particles. Lower it if you run out of memory. --threads int 8 Reader threads feeding the GPU with image chunks. On a spinning disk (HDD), several threads read different regions of the stack at once and the head seeks between them — try 1 or 2 there, it is often faster than the default. --ssd_scratch_folder path — Folder on a fast (SSD/NVMe) disk where the particles are cached as a local float16 copy (half the bytes) and streamed from. See the note below.

If your particles live on a slow disk, the read is the run

This program touches every particle exactly once, so its wall clock is set by how fast the images arrive. 1M particles at box 320 is 410 GB — about an hour off a spinning disk, during which the GPU sits idle. --ssd_scratch_folder caches the stack on fast storage as float16 and streams from there.

It does not make a single cold run faster: building the cache still costs one full read of the original stack. It pays off because the copy is reused — by later runs, and by the other hax programs (HetSIREN, Zernike3Deep, MoDART…) pointed at the same scratch folder, which build and read exactly the same cache. Whichever program runs first pays for it; everything after reads from the SSD. That matters most for the training programs, which re-read every particle every epoch.

docs.title: Example commands
docs.text:
Consensus map + mask from a posed, CTF-carrying particle set — the usual invocation:

hax_project_manager --gpu 0 reconstruct_volume \
    --md particles.xmd \
    --sr 1.5 \
    --ctf_type apply \
    --write_mask \
    --output_path consensus/

Raw map, with no FSC filtering and no gray-scale calibration (e.g. to inspect what the denoising is actually removing):

hax_project_manager --gpu 0 reconstruct_volume \
    --md particles.xmd \
    --sr 1.5 \
    --ctf_type apply \
    --no_denoise \
    --no_gray_scale_calibration \
    --output_path consensus_raw/

Already CTF-corrected images (e.g. coming from Preprocess Particles with --ctf_correction):

hax_project_manager --gpu 0 reconstruct_volume \
    --md preprocessed_particles.xmd \
    --sr 3.0 \
    --ctf_type None \
    --output_path consensus/

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
In --output_path:

  • consensus_reconstruction.mrc — the reconstructed map, FSC-filtered and gray-scale calibrated unless you disabled either.
  • consensus_mask.mrc — the binary mask derived from it, only with --write_mask.
  • run_config.json — the fully-resolved parameters of the run (reusable as a --config).

The measured resolution (half-map FSC = 0.143) is printed at the end of the run.

docs.title: Tips & pitfalls
docs.text:
• --ctf_type must match your data. Weighting CTF-free images by a CTF is not a harmless no-op — it reweights the slices and visibly degrades the map. If your images were already CTF-corrected during preprocessing, pass --ctf_type None.
  • The poses have to be right. This program trusts the alignments in --md completely; it does not refine them. If the map comes out as a featureless blob, suspect the poses first — ReconSIREN can estimate them ab initio.
  • The map is deliberately not sharpened: it is filtered to the resolution the two halves actually agree on. That is what makes it safe as a reference — noise in it would otherwise propagate straight into the mask and into everything trained against it.
  • Feed the resulting map and mask into HetSIREN / Zernike3Deep (--vol / --mask) rather than only the map: the mask is what gives the deformation somewhere to act.
  • If the run feels slow, watch nvidia-smi before tuning anything. A GPU that idles and spikes is starved by the disk, not short of compute — and no parameter here will change that. Reach for --ssd_scratch_folder, a lower --threads, or a smaller box via Preprocess Particles.

docs.title: Volume Gray-Scale Adjustment
docs.text:
At a glance

CLI name: volume_gray_scale_adjustment · Family: Gray-scale adjustment · Trains a network: no · Modes: none (a single pass over the particles)

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
A map obtained elsewhere (another program, another data set, a simulation) is rarely on the gray scale of your particles. Volume Gray-Scale Adjustment finds the single scale that makes the projections of the map match the images, and applies it to the map.

The map is projected at the pose of every particle, with its shift and CTF applied, and the scale is the least-squares fit of all the images to those projections, solved in closed form. The output is the input map multiplied by that scale: nothing is resampled, masked or fitted with Gaussians, and no offset is added (a constant in the map would also fill the background).

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• Before using a map as the reference of a program that compares its projections with the images (HetSIREN, Zernike3Deep, MoDART...), when the map does not come from these particles.
  • To compare or combine maps from different sources on the gray scale of the same images.

docs.title: Required
docs.text: Option Type Description --md path Metadata file with the images, their poses and CTF — Xmipp .xmd, Relion .star, or CryoSPARC .cs (read directly). --vol path Map to adjust. It must have the same box and sampling rate as the images. --sr float Sampling rate (pixel size), in Å/px. --ctf_type choice None, apply, wiener, precorrect or premultiplied (as in Image Gray-Scale Adjustment). --output_path path Folder where results are saved (created if needed).

docs.title: Adjustment
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --fit_offset flag off Allow an offset per image while fitting the scale. Use it when the images are not normalized to a zero-mean background. The offsets are not applied to the map. --mask path — Binary mask of the region to match. The fit then only uses the pixels inside the projection of the mask. The scale is applied to the whole map either way.

docs.title: Data loading
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --batch_size int 256 Images read and projected at once. Lower it if the GPU runs out of memory; it does not change the result. --threads int 8 Reader threads feeding the GPU. On a spinning disk, 1 or 2 can be faster. --ssd_scratch_folder path — Fast-disk folder where the images are cached (as float16) and read from — the same cache the other Hax programs build there.

docs.title: Example command
docs.text:
hax_project_manager --gpu 0 volume_gray_scale_adjustment \
    --md particles.xmd \
    --vol reference.mrc \
    --sr 1.5 \
    --ctf_type apply \
    --output_path vol_adjust/

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
• adjusted_volume.mrc — the input map multiplied by the fitted scale.
  • gray_scale.txt — the scale itself, so it can be applied to other copies of the map (for example, the same map at a different box).

docs.title: Tips & pitfalls
docs.text:
• The fit needs reliable poses and the right CTF type. If the projections come out anti-correlated with the images, the program stops: check that the images and the map have the same contrast (protein white) and that --ctf_type matches the data.
  • Every particle is used, so the scale is very precise; what limits it is how well the map and the poses describe the data.
  • Reconstruct Volume already calibrates the gray scale of the maps it reconstructs, so they do not need this step.
  • For a per-particle correction instead, see Image Gray-Scale Adjustment.

docs.title: Zernike3Deep
docs.text:
At a glance

CLI name: zernike3deep · Family: Heterogeneity analysis · Trains a network: yes · Modes: train, predict

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
Zernike3Deep estimates the continuous motions of your molecule by deforming a reference volume to match each particle image. The deformation is expressed in the mathematically compact 3D Zernike polynomial basis, which describes smooth, physically plausible movements with relatively few coefficients.

You provide a reference volume and your particles; Zernike3Deep learns, for every particle, the set of Zernike coefficients that warps the reference into that particle's conformation. Those coefficients form the latent space — your conformational landscape. It is a semi-classical approach: a neural network drives a well-understood, interpretable deformation model.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: Herreros, D., Lederman, R.R., Krieger, J.M. et al. Estimating conformational landscapes from Cryo-EM particles by 3D Zernike polynomials. Nature Communications 14, 154 (2023). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-35791-y

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• You have a good reference volume and want to model smooth, continuous deformations.
  • You want an interpretable motion model (Zernike coefficients) rather than a fully implicit one.
  • You plan to feed the result into MoDART for motion-corrected reconstruction, or into Estimate Latent Covariances → Latent Space Deconvolution.

If you do not have a reliable reference, or you need fully real-space implicit reconstruction, consider HetSIREN instead.

Zernike3Deep also accepts tomography (subtomogram) data: if the input metadata contains subtomo_labels, each particle's tilt stack is analyzed as one item.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: You can also pass any of these options through a YAML/JSON file with --config (see The Command Line).

docs.title: Required
docs.text: Option Type Description --md path Metadata file with the images (plus alignments / CTF) — Xmipp .xmd, Relion .star, or CryoSPARC .cs (read directly). --vol path The reference volume to be warped towards the images. --sr float Sampling rate (pixel size), in Å/px. --ctf_type choice None, apply, wiener, precorrect or premultiplied (images that already carry one CTF multiplication, as in many tomography exports). See Core Concepts. --mode choice train or predict (predict needs --reload). --output_path path Folder where all results are saved.

docs.title: Deformation model
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --mask path auto Binary mask enclosing all the mass that may move. If omitted, the volume is masked automatically (saved as mask.mrc). --lat_dim int 8 Dimensionality of the latent space. --L1 int 7 Degree of the Zernike3D radial component. Higher captures more localized motion at higher memory cost. --L2 int 7 Degree of the Zernike3D angular component. Higher captures more localized motion at higher memory cost. --basis choice zernike Deformation basis. zernike: global Zernike3D polynomials (--L1, --L2); patches: blended local affine patches over the Gaussians, more local motion per coefficient (e.g. domain motions around hinges). --num_patches int 30 Number of patches of --basis patches (4 coefficients per patch and axis). --patch_width float 0.4 Width of the patch blending weights of --basis patches, as a fraction of the mean spacing between patch centres. --patch_rigidity float 0.0 Weight, relative to the edge strain, of a penalty on the stretch and shear of each patch of --basis patches (Green strain of its local affine fit), so patches move rigidly. Part of the deformation prior scaled by --deformation_strength; 0 disables it. --num_gaussians int auto Number of Gaussians fitted to the reference volume before training. By default the count is grown until the fit reaches FSC ≥ 0.5 on every populated shell (see --fit_resolution); set it to fix the number yourself (e.g. to the residue count). --fit_resolution float — Resolution (Å) the automatic Gaussian fit has to reproduce. --deformation_strength float 0.3 Strength of the graph deformation priors (relative edge strain + repulsion) with respect to the reconstruction loss. After the first epoch the prior weight is set once (then kept fixed) so its gradient on the decoder is this fraction of the reconstruction gradient. Lower for larger motions, higher for stiffer ones; 0 disables it. --strain_penalty choice huber Penalty on the relative edge strain. huber: grows without limit with the strain; bounded: saturates, so domains stay rigid while a contact between them can open at a fixed cost.

docs.title: Latent regularization
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --kl_lambda float 0.0 Weight of the VAE KL divergence towards a standard-normal prior (summed over the batch and the latent dimensions; 1e-6 was the previous built-in value). 0 disables the VAE and uses a deterministic latent. --decoupling_lambda float 1e-4 Weight of the decoupling regularization encouraging the latent to be invariant to pose and CTF. Increase for stronger decoupling; 0 to relax. --nested_dropout float 0.0 Nested dropout on the decoded latent: during training each sample keeps only its first k latent dimensions, with k drawn from a Geometric(p) distribution. This orders the dimensions by importance (PCA-like), so the first ones carry the dominant motions. Typical 0.1–0.5; 0 disables it. --noise_invariance_strength float 0.0 Penalizes latent dimensions that change when the noise changes: each image is encoded again with a second draw of noise, colored like the image background, and the loss is 1 − correlation between both latents, per dimension. After the first epoch its weight is recalibrated every epoch so its encoder gradient is this fraction of the reconstruction one. Typical 0.1–0.5; 0 disables it. Ignored for tomography data.

docs.title: Pose refinement
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --pose_refine_reg float 0.1 Weight of the hinge penalizing pose refinements beyond --pose_refine_max_angle. 0 disables it. --pose_refine_max_angle float 8.0 Rotation (degrees) the pose refinement may apply freely; the excess is penalized with --pose_refine_reg. --shift_refine_reg float 0.1 Weight of the hinge penalizing shift refinements beyond --shift_refine_max. 0 disables it. --shift_refine_max float 4.0 Shift (pixels) the refinement may apply freely; the excess is penalized with --shift_refine_reg. --rigid_gauge choice core Remove the global rigid motion from the deformation field so pose errors go to the pose head. core: frame fitted on the least-moving points; mass: mass-weighted fit; off: diagnostic only. --rigid_drift_lambda float 1.0 Weight of the penalty on the rigid motion the gauge removes from the deformation field.

docs.title: Images
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --normalize_images flag off Normalize each particle (zero mean, unit std in the background outside the particle) before the encoder, the loss and the contrast fit of the Gaussians. --particle_diameter float auto Particle diameter (Å), used as the background for --normalize_images and for the soft circular mask of the images. Default: the extent of the mask. --per_image_contrast choice off Fit one contrast scale per image before the reconstruction loss. relative: scales normalized to a unit batch mean; absolute: raw least-squares scale.

docs.title: Training control
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --epochs int 50 Passes over the dataset (~50–100 for ≈100k particles). --batch_size int / auto 8 Images on the GPU at once (GPU-memory lever). auto estimates the largest batch that fits on your GPU, capped at the number of particles (tomography data and predict fall back to 8). --learning_rate float 1e-4 Step size of learning; lower ~10× if it diverges. --dataset_split_fraction list 0.8,0.2 Train/validation split (must sum to 1). --reload path — A saved network to fine-tune or to run predict. Because Zernike3Deep also learns a gray-level adjustment, this folder must contain both Zernike3Deep and Gaussian_volume_fitting subfolders.

docs.title: Reference update
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --refit_reference flag off With --reload in train mode: fit the Gaussians to --vol (e.g. a MoDART map) and fine-tune the reloaded network on them. The architecture of the reloaded network is kept, and every weight whose shape still matches is reused. A patch basis keeps its patch centres, so the reloaded coefficients keep their meaning. MoDART's --refine_iterations runs this fine-tune for you.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --log_images_every int 1 Epochs between the cheap TensorBoard logs (predicted images, central slices of the predicted volumes). 0 disables them. --log_landscape_every int 5 Epochs between the expensive logs (latent-space embedding, intermediate volumes, angular distribution plots). Raise it if logging dominates the training time on small datasets; 0 disables them. --log_checkpoint_every int 5 Epochs between the checkpoints used to resume an interrupted training. 0 disables them. --log_time_budget float 0.0 Maximum fraction of the wall clock that may be spent logging (e.g. 0.05); above it the expensive logs are skipped until training catches up. 0 disables the guard. --log_sync flag off Log on the training thread instead of a background thread (useful for debugging).

docs.title: Data loading
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --load_images_to_ram flag off Load all images into RAM (fastest). Otherwise memory-mapped. --ssd_scratch_folder path — Fast-SSD folder used when memory-mapping.

docs.title: Example commands
docs.text:
Train a Zernike3D landscape from a reference and particles:

hax_project_manager --gpu 0 zernike3deep \
    --md particles.xmd \
    --vol reference.mrc \
    --sr 1.5 \
    --ctf_type apply \
    --mode train \
    --lat_dim 8 --L1 7 --L2 7 \
    --epochs 80 \
    --output_path zernike_run/

Predict the per-particle coefficients with the trained network:

hax_project_manager --gpu 0 zernike3deep \
    --md particles.xmd \
    --vol reference.mrc \
    --sr 1.5 \
    --ctf_type apply \
    --mode predict \
    --reload zernike_run/ \
    --output_path zernike_predict/

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
After training:

  • Zernike3Deep/ — the trained network.
  • Zernike3Deep_metrics/ — training/validation curves and volume slices.
  • Intermediate_volumes/ — volumes decoded at cluster centres of the latent space, written every --log_landscape_every epochs.
  • Gaussian_volume_fitting/, consensus_volume.mrc, consensus_volume_deltas.mrc — the Gaussian fit used internally.
  • mask.mrc — the auto-generated mask, when you did not supply one.
  • Zernike3Deep_CHECKPOINT/ — intermediate checkpoint (removed on clean completion).
  • run_config.json — the fully-resolved parameters of the run (reusable as a --config).

After predict:

  • predicted_latents.xmd / .star — metadata with the latent coefficients and refined poses for every particle.

docs.title: Tips & pitfalls
docs.text:
• A reference volume is mandatory — Zernike3Deep deforms it. Make sure --sr matches both the volume and the images.
  • Increase --L1 / --L2 to chase very localized motions, but watch GPU memory. For domain motions around hinges, --basis patches gives more local motion per coefficient; add --patch_rigidity to keep each patch rigid.
  • Domains that should move as rigid blocks? Try --strain_penalty bounded, and lower --deformation_strength for large-amplitude motions.
  • To get a compact, ordered latent space, combine --nested_dropout with --noise_invariance_strength (e.g. 0.1–0.5 each). The current noise-invariance loss and weight are shown in the progress bar (noise_inv=loss/weight) and logged as Noise invariance (Zernike3Deep) in the training metrics.
  • The network saved by a train run can be reused directly by Estimate Latent Covariances, Decode States from Latents and MoDART — just point them at the Zernike3Deep folder inside your output.

docs.title: Contact & Support
docs.text: Hax is developed in the open. Whether you hit a bug, have a question, or want to suggest an improvement, we'd love to hear from you.

docs.title: Report an issue or ask a question
docs.text:
The best place for bug reports, questions and feature requests is the project's GitHub issue tracker:

Open an issue on GitHub Browse the repository

Before opening a new issue, it helps to search the existing ones — your question may already be answered.

docs.title: Writing a useful bug report
docs.text:
To help us reproduce and fix a problem quickly, please include:

  • What you ran — the full hax_project_manager … command line.
  • What happened — the full error message / traceback, copied as text.
  • What you expected to happen instead.
  • Your environment — Hax version (python -c "import hax; print(hax.__version__)"), the CUDA extra you installed (cuda12/cuda13), your GPU and NVIDIA driver version (nvidia-smi).
  • Data shape, when relevant — number of particles, box size, sampling rate.

Check the metrics first

If a training run behaved oddly, the curves shown by Display Metrics often reveal what went wrong (e.g. a diverging loss pointing at too high a learning rate). Attaching a screenshot can speed up diagnosis.

docs.title: Report a graphical interface (GUI) issue or improvement
docs.text:
Problems, questions and suggestions about the Hax graphical interface belong in its own GitHub issue tracker, which is separate from the core hax-em one:

Open an issue on GitHub Browse the repository

As above, please search the existing issues before opening a new one — someone may have already reported the same thing.

docs.title: Writing a useful GUI report
docs.text:
Because the interface is visual, screenshots are the single most helpful thing you can attach — both for bugs and for improvement ideas:

  • Screenshots — capture the screen showing the problem (or the part you'd like to see improved). For a bug, include the moment the error or unexpected behaviour appears; for a suggestion, mark up the screenshot to show what you have in mind. You can drag-and-drop images straight into the GitHub issue text box.
  • What you were doing — the steps that led to the issue (which panel, which buttons, which program you were launching).
  • What happened vs. what you expected to happen instead.
  • Any error text — messages shown in the interface, and anything printed in the terminal / console the GUI was started from (copied as text).
  • Your environment — the GUI version, your operating system and browser (if you use the web interface), and the Hax version (python -c "import hax; print(hax.__version__)").

Capturing a screenshot

On most systems: Windows — Win+Shift+S; macOS — Cmd+Shift+4; Linux — the Screenshot utility or Print. Recording a short screen capture (GIF or video) is even better when the problem only shows up while interacting with the interface.
