docs.title: Real-Case Examples
docs.text:
This page walks through complete, end-to-end sessions that combine several Hax programs. They are written to be realistic and copy-paste-friendly.

These examples are illustrative

File names (particles.xmd, reference.mrc, …), pixel sizes and epoch counts are placeholders. Replace them with your own data and tune the numbers to your dataset size and hardware. The structure of each workflow — the order of programs and how their outputs feed each other — is what matters.

Conventions used below

  • --gpu 0 runs everything on the first GPU; change as needed.
  • We assume a sampling rate of 1.5 Å/px and CTF handling with apply.
  • Each step writes into its own output folder so nothing is overwritten.
  • The --md files are written as .xmd here, but Relion .star and CryoSPARC .cs files work just as well — pass them directly.

docs.title: Example 1 — Continuous heterogeneity with Zernike3Deep + MoDART
docs.text: Goal: starting from aligned particles and a consensus map, estimate the continuous motion of a flexible complex, explore it, and reconstruct a motion-corrected map.

docs.title: Step 0 · (optional) Preprocess to fit your GPU
docs.text:
If a 256-box does not fit, or you just want the exploration to go faster, shrink the particles and the volumes to a 128-box before anything else:

hax_project_manager --gpu 0 preprocess_particles \
    --md particles.xmd \
    --sr 1.5 \
    --new_box_size 128 \
    --output_path 00_preprocessed/

hax_project_manager preprocess_volumes \
    --vol reference.mrc mask.mrc \
    --sr 1.5 \
    --new_box_size 128 \
    --output_path 00_preprocessed/

This costs resolution — the Nyquist limit moves from 3.0 Å to 6.0 Å — and buys roughly 4× less VRAM and a proportionally faster run. See Stage 0.

If you take this route, substitute throughout the rest of the example

--md 00_preprocessed/preprocessed_particles.xmd, --vol 00_preprocessed/reference_preprocessed.mrc, --mask 00_preprocessed/mask_preprocessed.mrc, and --sr 3.0 instead of 1.5. The steps below are written against the original, full-size files.

docs.title: Step 1 · Train the motion model
docs.text:
hax_project_manager --gpu 0 zernike3deep \
    --md particles.xmd \
    --vol reference.mrc \
    --mask mask.mrc \
    --sr 1.5 \
    --ctf_type apply \
    --mode train \
    --lat_dim 8 --L1 7 --L2 7 \
    --epochs 80 \
    --output_path 01_zernike_train/

Monitor it while it runs:

hax_project_manager display_metrics --logdir 01_zernike_train/Zernike3Deep_metrics

docs.title: Step 2 · Predict the landscape
docs.text:
hax_project_manager --gpu 0 zernike3deep \
    --md particles.xmd \
    --vol reference.mrc \
    --sr 1.5 \
    --ctf_type apply \
    --mode predict \
    --reload 01_zernike_train/ \
    --output_path 02_zernike_predict/

This produces 02_zernike_predict/predicted_latents.xmd and the corresponding latent vectors.

docs.title: Step 3 · Clean the landscape
docs.text:
hax_project_manager --gpu 0 filter_latents \
    --latents 02_zernike_predict/latents.npy \
    --thr 1.0 --n_neighbours 10 \
    --output_path 03_filtered/

docs.title: Step 4 · Explore and select states
docs.text:
hax_project_manager annotate_space \
    --z_space 03_filtered/filtered_latents.npy \
    --path 04_annotation/ \
    --only_view

Use the viewer to identify clusters / a motion trajectory and export the latent vectors of interest (e.g. to selected_states.txt).

docs.title: Step 5 · Decode the selected states into volumes
docs.text:
Point the decoder straight at the network folder saved by the training run:

hax_project_manager --gpu 0 decode_states_from_latents \
    --latents_file 04_annotation/selected_states.txt \
    --reload 01_zernike_train/Zernike3Deep \
    --output_path 06_decoded/

docs.title: Step 6 · Motion-corrected reconstruction
docs.text:
hax_project_manager --gpu 0 modart \
    --md particles.xmd \
    --sr 1.5 \
    --ctf_type apply \
    --motion_correction 01_zernike_train/Zernike3Deep \
    --reconstruct_halves \
    --output_path 07_modart/

You now have 07_modart/modart_map.mrc (and half-maps for resolution estimation) that is sharper in the flexible regions than a plain average would be. 07_modart/half_map_fsc.txt holds the half-map FSC that filtered it.

docs.title: Example 2 — Real-space heterogeneous reconstruction with HetSIREN
docs.text: Goal: without necessarily having a perfect reference, recover and disentangle conformational states directly in real space, then materialize representative maps.

docs.title: Step 1 · Train HetSIREN
docs.text:
hax_project_manager --gpu 0 hetsiren \
    --md particles.xmd \
    --mask roi_mask.mrc \
    --sr 1.5 \
    --ctf_type apply \
    --mode train \
    --lat_dim 8 \
    --epochs 100 \
    --output_path 01_hetsiren_train/

To model motion explicitly (helpful for large boxes), add --transport_mass and use a tight mask. For very local motions, consider --implicit_network.

docs.title: Step 2 · Predict the landscape
docs.text:
hax_project_manager --gpu 0 hetsiren \
    --md particles.xmd \
    --sr 1.5 \
    --ctf_type apply \
    --mode predict \
    --reload 01_hetsiren_train/ \
    --output_path 02_hetsiren_predict/

docs.title: Step 3 · Explore interactively (with live volume generation)
docs.text:
hax_project_manager annotate_space \
    --z_space 02_hetsiren_predict/latents.npy \
    --env_name hax \
    --server_functions_path my_hetsiren_loader.py \
    --chimerax_binary /opt/chimerax/bin/ChimeraX \
    --path 03_annotation/

Here the viewer regenerates the 3D map for any point you hover, displaying it live in ChimeraX. The my_hetsiren_loader.py file follows the example shipped in the package source (hax/viewers/server_loading_functions/load_model.py).

docs.title: Step 4 · Decode a trajectory of states
docs.text:
hax_project_manager --gpu 0 decode_states_from_latents \
    --latents_file 03_annotation/trajectory.txt \
    --reload 01_hetsiren_train/HetSIREN \
    --output_path 05_trajectory_volumes/

The resulting decoded_volume_*.mrc series is a "movie" of the conformational change.

docs.title: Example 3 — Validating a landscape with FlexConsensus + deconvolution
docs.text: Goal: you ran two heterogeneity methods on the same particles and want a single, trustworthy, sharpened landscape.

docs.title: Step 1 · Produce two landscapes for the same particles
docs.text:
Run, for example, Zernike3Deep and HetSIREN in predict mode on the same, identically-ordered particle set, giving zernike_latents.npy and hetsiren_latents.npy.

Same particles, same order

FlexConsensus requires every input space to have the same number of vectors, in the same order. Export both from the same particle list.

docs.title: Step 2 · Merge them into a consensus space
docs.text:
hax_project_manager --gpu 0 flexconsensus \
    --input_space Zernike:zernike_latents.npy \
    --input_space HetSIREN:hetsiren_latents.npy \
    --mode train \
    --epochs 150 \
    --output_path 01_flexconsensus_train/

hax_project_manager --gpu 0 flexconsensus \
    --input_space Zernike:zernike_latents.npy \
    --input_space HetSIREN:hetsiren_latents.npy \
    --mode predict \
    --reload 01_flexconsensus_train/ \
    --output_path 02_flexconsensus_predict/

The *_consensus_error.npy / *_representation_error.npy files tell you where the two methods agree and where they don't.

docs.title: Step 3 · Sharpen the landscape by deconvolution
docs.text:
# Estimate the per-particle covariances from the trained network
hax_project_manager --gpu 0 estimate_latent_covariances \
    --md particles.xmd \
    --nn_path zernike_run/Zernike3Deep \
    --output_path 04_covariances/

# Deconvolve
hax_project_manager --gpu 0 latent_space_deconvolution \
    --md particles.xmd \
    --nn_path zernike_run/Zernike3Deep \
    --covariances 04_covariances/covariance_matrices.npy \
    --mode train \
    --output_path 05_deconv_train/

hax_project_manager --gpu 0 latent_space_deconvolution \
    --md particles.xmd \
    --nn_path zernike_run/Zernike3Deep \
    --covariances 04_covariances/covariance_matrices.npy \
    --mode predict \
    --reload 05_deconv_train/ \
    --output_path 06_deconv_predict/

06_deconv_predict/latents_deconvolved.npy is your final, sharpened landscape — ready to explore with Annotate Space.

docs.title: Choosing a path quickly
docs.text: If you want to… Start here Get poses / an initial map from scratch ReconSIREN Build a consensus map from particles you already posed Reconstruct Volume Model smooth motion from a good reference Zernike3Deep Do flexible real-space reconstruction HetSIREN Merge / validate multiple landscapes FlexConsensus Remove estimation blur from a landscape Latent Space Deconvolution See and select conformations Annotate Space Get a sharp, motion-corrected map MoDART

docs.title: Pipelines
docs.text:
Hax programs are designed to be chained. The output of one is the input of the next: a metadata file becomes a landscape, a landscape becomes states, states become motion-corrected maps. This page shows how the pieces fit together so you can plan a project end to end.

Read this alongside the Programs overview

Each box below links to the program that performs it. For runnable, copy-paste sequences see Real-Case Examples.

docs.title: The big picture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Particle images + metadata<br/>.xmd / .star / .cs] --> P{Box too big for<br/>your GPU or budget?}
    P -- Yes --> Q[Preprocess Particles + Volumes<br/>smaller box, optional CTF correction]
    P -- No --> B{Have reliable<br/>poses & a map?}
    Q --> B
    B -- No poses --> C[ReconSIREN<br/>ab initio pose / shift + initial volume]
    B -- Poses, no map --> R[Reconstruct Volume<br/>consensus map + mask from the poses]
    B -- Yes --> D[Heterogeneity analysis]
    C --> D
    R --> D

    D --> E[Zernike3Deep<br/>continuous motion from a reference]
    D --> F[HetSIREN<br/>real-space heterogeneous reconstruction]

    E --> G[predicted_latents<br/>latent space]
    F --> G

    G --> H[Filter Latents<br/>remove outliers]
    H --> I[Annotate Space<br/>explore & select states]
    I --> J[Decode States from Latents<br/>latent vectors -> volumes]

    E --> K[MoDART<br/>motion-corrected reconstruction]
    F --> K
    J --> L[Final volumes / movies]
    K --> L

docs.title: Stage 0 — Preprocess (optional, but often worth it)
docs.text:
Everything downstream reads the same particles over and over. Shrinking them once is the cheapest lever you have on VRAM and wall-clock time — and the one that costs you resolution, so spend it deliberately.

  • Preprocess Particles — crop and/or downsample the stack, and optionally correct the CTF (Wiener or phase flip) once instead of every epoch.
  • Preprocess Volumes — put the reference map and its mask on the same box and sampling rate.

Halving the box divides the pixel count — and roughly the memory a network needs — by four, while training gets correspondingly faster. What you give up is resolution: the new Nyquist frequency becomes 2 × sr × box_in / box_out Å, and no downstream program can recover detail beyond it. A common, honest strategy is to explore on a small box and, once the landscape and the parameters are settled, repeat the final run at full size.

flowchart LR
    A[particles.xmd<br/>256 box @ 1.5 A/px] --> B[Preprocess Particles<br/>--new_box_size 128]
    C[reference.mrc + mask.mrc] --> D[Preprocess Volumes<br/>--new_box_size 128]
    B --> E[128 box @ 3.0 A/px<br/>4x less VRAM]
    D --> E
    E --> F[Stage 1 / Stage 2]

Three things to carry forward

  • Pass the new --sr (printed by the program) to every downstream run.
  • If you used --ctf_correction, run downstream programs with --ctf_type None — the images are already corrected, and doing it twice corrupts the analysis.
  • Preprocess the volume and the mask with the same settings as the particles, or the projections will not line up with the images.

If preprocessing itself runs out of memory

Preprocessing a large box is the one step that can OOM before you have shrunk anything. Pass --batch_size auto to Preprocess Particles and it will size the batch to your card analytically. It exists to make a big box fit, not to go faster.

docs.title: Stage 1 — Get a starting point
docs.text:
Before studying motion, you need decent poses (orientations + shifts) and, ideally, a consensus map.

  • If your particles already have a good alignment from an upstream package (Relion, Xmipp, cryoSPARC…) and a reference map, you can go straight to Stage 2.
  • If they have good poses but no map (or one you do not trust), build one with Reconstruct Volume: the poses alone are enough to recover a consensus map in a single pass, together with the mask derived from it. It reports the resolution it reached (half-map FSC), so you know what you are handing to Stage 2.
  • If the poses themselves are missing or unreliable, use ReconSIREN for an ab initio assignment and an initial volume.
flowchart LR
    A[Raw particles] --> B[ReconSIREN]
    B --> C[poses + shifts]
    B --> D[reconsiren_map.mrc]
    E[Posed particles] --> F[Reconstruct Volume]
    F --> G[consensus_reconstruction.mrc<br/>+ consensus_mask.mrc]

HetSIREN will do it for you

Launched with neither --vol nor --mask, HetSIREN runs this same reconstruction internally. Doing it as an explicit step is worth it when you want to inspect the reference first, tune the mask, or reuse one reference across several runs.

docs.title: Stage 2 — Estimate the conformational landscape
docs.text:
This is the heart of Hax. Pick the method that matches your situation:

Choose… When Zernike3Deep You have a good reference volume and want smooth, interpretable deformations (and want to feed MoDART later). HetSIREN You want flexible, high-fidelity real-space heterogeneous reconstruction, with optional mass transport / local refinement.

Both produce, after a predict run, a latent space describing every particle's conformation (predicted_latents.xmd/.star, and a .npy of the latent vectors).

flowchart LR
    A[particles + reference] --> B[Zernike3Deep / HetSIREN<br/>mode: train]
    B --> C[trained network]
    C --> D[mode: predict]
    D --> E[predicted_latents<br/>latent space]

docs.title: Stage 3 — Clean, merge and sharpen the landscape
docs.text:
Optional refinements that make the landscape more trustworthy:

  • Filter Latents — drop outlier particles.
  • FlexConsensus — merge landscapes from several methods into one consensus space (and check what is reproducible).
  • Estimate Latent Covariances → Latent Space Deconvolution — remove the estimation blur so distinct states separate cleanly.
flowchart TD
    A[latent space] --> B[Filter Latents]
    A --> C[Estimate Latent Covariances]
    C --> D[Latent Space Deconvolution]
    M1[method 1 latents] --> E[FlexConsensus]
    M2[method 2 latents] --> E
    E --> F[consensus space]
    B --> G[cleaner landscape]
    D --> G
    F --> G

docs.title: Stage 4 — Explore and materialize states
docs.text:
• Annotate Space — explore the landscape interactively, cluster it, and select the conformations you care about.
  • Decode States from Latents — turn the selected latent vectors (cluster centres, a trajectory, …) into 3D volumes.
flowchart LR
    A[cleaned landscape] --> B[Annotate Space<br/>select / cluster]
    B --> C[latent vectors]
    C --> D[Decode States from Latents]
    D --> E[volumes / movie]

docs.title: Stage 5 — Motion-corrected reconstruction
docs.text:
To obtain a sharp map that is not blurred by flexibility, feed a motion model (Zernike3Deep, or HetSIREN trained with transport of mass) into MoDART.

flowchart LR
    A[particles] --> C[MoDART]
    B[Zernike3Deep / HetSIREN<br/>motion model] --> C
    C --> D[modart_map.mrc, FSC-filtered<br/>+ optional half-maps]
    D -.->|refit reference| B

Keep the consensus map from Stage 1 around: reconstructed from the same particles with the flexibility averaged away, it is the honest baseline against which to judge how much MoDART actually sharpened.

Give MoDART the particles with the poses the motion model was trained on: it adds the network's pose refinement on top of them. Particles from a predict run already carry that refinement: pass them with --poses_refined_by <network>. The MoDART map can go back in as a sharper reference: fine-tune the same network on it with --reload and --refit_reference, then reconstruct again. MoDART's --refine_iterations repeats this loop for you (iterative refinement).

docs.title: Supporting steps you can drop in anywhere
docs.text:
• Display Metrics — monitor any training run's curves.
  • Image / Volume Gray-Scale Adjustment — match intensity levels when comparing or combining maps and images.
